The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: Reducing Bias in Sentiment Analysis Models Through Causal Mediation Analysis and Targeted Counterfactual Training
papers.research_question: How to reduce bias in sentiment analysis models by leveraging causal mediation analysis to identify biased components and applying targeted counterfactual training for de-biasing.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a bias reduction method for sentiment analysis models that uses causal mediation analysis to identify layers causally implicated in gender bias and then applies counterfactual training only to those targeted layers, achieving improved fairness without loss of accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method successfully reduces gender bias in BERT sentiment models by using causal mediation analysis to target specific layers and then applying counterfactual training, resulting in improved fairness without compromising accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Causal mediation analysis can identify specific layers in BERT that contribute to gender bias.
Targeted counterfactual training on those identified layers reduces bias effectively.
The proposed method achieves higher fairness (lower Wasserstein distance) compared to baseline methods like full-model counterfactual training and dropout regularization.
The method maintains sentiment prediction accuracy while improving fairness, avoiding the accuracy-fairness trade-off.
The approach is validated on two sentiment analysis datasets (SST-2 and Amazon reviews) and evaluated on the Equity Evaluation Corpus (EEC).
papers.limitation: Limited to two datasets (SST-2 and Amazon reviews) and one fairness metric (p-Wasserstein).
future_direction: Apply the method to other biases on sensitive attributes such as ethnic groups, skin colour, and country.
Test the method on a broader range of datasets and with more fairness evaluation techniques.
Quantify the accuracy-fairness trade-off in real-world datasets.
papers.abstract: Large language models provide high-accuracy solutions in many natural language processing tasks. In particular, they are used as word embeddings in sentiment analysis models. However, these models pick up on and amplify biases and social stereotypes in the data. Causality theory has recently driven the development of effective algorithms to evaluate and mitigate these biases. Causal mediation was used to detect biases, while counterfactual training was proposed to mitigate bias. In both cases, counterfactual sentences are created by changing an attribute, such as the gender of a noun, for which no change in the model output is expected. Biases are detected and eventually corrected each time the model behaviour differs between the original and the counterfactual sentence. We propose a new method for de-biasing sentiment analysis models that leverages the causal mediation analysis to identify the parts of the model primarily responsible for the bias and apply targeted counterfactual training for model de-biasing. We validated the methodology by fine-tuning the pre-trained Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model for sentiment prediction. We trained two sentiment analysis models using the Stanford Sentiment Treebank dataset and the Amazon Product Reviews, respectively, and we evaluated the fairness and prediction performances using the Equity Evaluation Corpus. We illustrated the causal patterns in the network and showed that our method achieves both high fairness and more accurate sentiment analysis than the state-of-the-art approach. Contrary to state-of-the-art models, we achieved a noticeable improvement in gender fairness without hindering sentiment prediction accuracy.

papers.title: Monolingual and Multilingual Reduction of Gender Bias in Contextualized Representations
papers.research_question: How can we effectively reduce gender bias in contextualized representations using DensRay, and how is gender information distributed in BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using DensRay to debias contextualized representations, showing it performs comparably to prior methods, is more robust, preserves language model performance better, and enables multilingual debiasing.
papers.conclusion: DensRay is an effective method for reducing gender bias in contextualized representations, maintaining model performance, and can be applied multilingually.
papers.key_findings:
DensRay effectively mitigates gender bias on OCCTMP and association tests.
DensRay preserves language model performance on Wikitext-2 and GLUE tasks better than other methods.
Gender information is spread across all attention heads and most layers in BERT, with no single head responsible.
DensRay can obtain gender bias scores on token and sentence levels.
DensRay can be used for zero-shot multilingual debiasing (e.g., debias Chinese using English data).
papers.limitation:
Token-level bias scores work well for monolingual BERT but not for multilingual BERT.
The method focuses only on the gender direction and may not address biases from implicitly gendered terms.
future_direction: Investigate multilingual transfer of debiasing techniques more closely.
Investigate debiasing with non-binary approaches (beyond male-female binary).
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) learn stereotypes held by humans and reflected in text from their training corpora, including gender bias. When PLMs are used for downstream tasks such as picking candidates for a job, people's lives can be negatively affected by these learned stereotypes. Prior work usually identifies a linear gender subspace and removes gender information by eliminating the subspace. Following this line of work, we propose to use DensRay, an analytical method for obtaining interpretable dense subspaces. We show that DensRay performs on-par with prior approaches, but provide arguments that it is more robust and provide indications that it preserves language model performance better. By applying DensRay to attention heads and layers of BERT we show that gender information is spread across all attention heads and most of the layers. Also we show that DensRay can obtain gender bias scores on both token and sentence levels. Finally, we demonstrate that we can remove bias multilingually, e.g., from Chinese, using only English training data.

papers.title: Interpreting Multilingual and Document-Length Sensitive Relevance Computations in Neural Retrieval Models through Axiomatic Causal Interventions
papers.research_question: How do neural retrieval models encode task-relevant properties such as term frequency and document length, and do these encodings generalize across languages?
papers.core_contribution: This reproducibility study confirms that activation patching can isolate term frequency and document length computations in a neural retrieval model, showing term frequency information is stored across query term occurrences and later in the CLS token, and that these mechanisms generalize across languages.
papers.conclusion: The work reaffirms that the designed activation patching method can uncover specific mechanisms of relevance modeling, such as term frequency and document length encoding, but also shows the need for more robust interpretability approaches and focus on reproducibility.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patching can effectively isolate task-dependent behavior to specific components and tokens in neural retrieval models.
Term frequency information is stored across occurrences of the query term, with emphasis on the first positions in the document in early layers, and later this information is stored in the pooled representation of the CLS token.
Document length information is also stored at the CLS token in later layers.
The location of term frequency information generalizes across languages (Spanish and Chinese).
The specific attention heads identified for encoding term frequency in English do not show the same patterns in Spanish and Chinese.
papers.limitation:
The activation patching setup requires the model to almost always follow the axiom (e.g., TFC1, LNC1), which is not always the case, and the ranking metric does not account for unexpected cases where the perturbation does not have the expected effect.
The identified attention heads for term frequency encoding were only clearly found for English (TFC1-I append) and not for Spanish or Chinese, suggesting the model may process languages differently.
future_direction: Investigating circuits of components instead of singular modules to obtain a clearer picture of how information is processed.
Testing different ranking metrics and perturbations to gain a wider knowledge of the inner workings of neural retrieval models.
Identifying specific mechanisms across other tasks and languages.
papers.abstract: This reproducibility study analyzes and extends the paper "Axiomatic Causal Interventions for Reverse Engineering Relevance Computation in Neural Retrieval Models," which investigates how neural retrieval models encode task-relevant properties such as term frequency. We reproduce key experiments from the original paper, confirming that information on query terms is captured in the model encoding. We extend this work by applying activation patching to Spanish and Chinese datasets and by exploring whether document-length information is encoded in the model as well. Our results confirm that the designed activation patching method can isolate the behavior to specific components and tokens in neural retrieval models. Moreover, our findings indicate that the location of term frequency generalizes across languages and that in later layers, the information for sequence-level tasks is represented in the CLS token. The results highlight the need for further research into interpretability in information retrieval and reproducibility in machine learning research. Our code is available at https://github.com/OliverSavolainen/axiomatic-ir-reproduce.

papers.title: The First Impression Problem: Internal Bias Triggers Overthinking in Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Reasoning models often exhibit overthinking, characterized by redundant reasoning steps. We identify \emph{internal bias} elicited by the input question as a key trigger of such behavior. Upon encountering a problem, the model immediately forms a preliminary guess about the answer, which we term an internal bias since it may not be explicitly generated, and it arises without systematic reasoning. When this guess conflicts with its subsequent reasoning, the model tends to engage in excessive reflection, resulting in wasted computation. We validate the association between internal bias and overthinking across multiple models and diverse reasoning tasks. To demonstrate the causal relationship more rigorously, we conduct two counterfactual interventions, showing that removing the input question after the model reduces the redundant reasoning across various complex reasoning tasks, and manually injecting bias affects overthinking accordingly. Further interpretability experiments suggest that excessive attention to the input question serves as a key mechanism through which internal bias influences subsequent reasoning trajectories. Finally, we evaluated several methods aimed at mitigating overthinking, yet the influence of internal bias persisted under all conditions.

papers.title: Attention Speaks Volumes: Localizing and Mitigating Bias in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does bias emerge in large language models when provided with ambiguous comparative prompts, and how can it be localized and mitigated by analyzing attention scores?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ATLAS, a two-step method to localize bias to specific layers via attention score analysis and mitigate it by scaling attention in those layers, reducing bias without significantly degrading model fluency.
papers.conclusion: ATLAS provides an effective approach for identifying and mitigating bias in LLMs when responding to ambiguous comparative prompts by localizing biased entity information to specific layers and scaling attention scores in those layers.
papers.key_findings:
Bias in LLMs is concentrated in the later layers, typically around the last third of the model's depth.
ATLAS effectively reduces bias across multiple models and datasets, improving the Exponential Bias Score (EBS).
The scaling intervention in ATLAS changes the model's preferred output candidate for a large fraction of prompts, demonstrating its effectiveness.
ATLAS outperforms baseline methods like PASTA (attention steering) and fairness persona prompting in bias reduction.
The intervention has minimal impact on model perplexity, indicating preserved response quality.
papers.limitation:
ATLAS is designed for the comparative prompting framework with two entities.
Determining the optimal scaling factor requires multiple inference calls, which is computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: We explore the internal mechanisms of how bias emerges in large language models (LLMs) when provided with ambiguous comparative prompts: inputs that compare or enforce choosing between two or more entities without providing clear context for preference. Most approaches for bias mitigation focus on either post-hoc analysis or data augmentation. However, these are transient solutions, without addressing the root cause: the model itself. Numerous prior works show the influence of the attention module towards steering generations. We believe that analyzing attention is also crucial for understanding bias, as it provides insight into how the LLM distributes its focus across different entities and how this contributes to biased decisions. To this end, we first introduce a metric to quantify the LLM's preference for one entity over another. We then propose $\texttt{ATLAS}$ (Attention-based Targeted Layer Analysis and Scaling), a technique to localize bias to specific layers of the LLM by analyzing attention scores and then reduce bias by scaling attention in these biased layers. To evaluate our method, we conduct experiments across 3 datasets (BBQ, Crows-Pairs, and WinoGender) using $\texttt{GPT-2 XL}$ (1.5B), $\texttt{GPT-J}$ (6B), $\texttt{LLaMA-2}$ (7B) and $\texttt{LLaMA-3}$ (8B). Our experiments demonstrate that bias is concentrated in the later layers, typically around the last third. We also show how $\texttt{ATLAS}$ effectively mitigates bias through targeted interventions without compromising downstream performance and an average increase of only 0.82% in perplexity when the intervention is applied. We see an average improvement of 0.28 points in the bias score across all the datasets.

papers.title: Quantifying and Mitigating Unimodal Biases in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: How do unimodal biases affect Multimodal Large Language Models in Visual Question Answering tasks, and how can they be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a causal framework to interpret unimodal biases in MLLMs, introduces the MORE dataset for evaluation, and develops the CAVE method to mitigate these biases.
papers.conclusion: The causal framework and MORE dataset provide insights into unimodal biases, and CAVE shows promise in enhancing MLLM reasoning, though challenges remain.
papers.key_findings:
MLLMs exhibit strong reliance on unimodal biases and perform poorly on the MORE dataset, not surpassing random baseline.
MLLMs struggle with multi-hop reasoning, especially as complexity increases.
GPT-4v is particularly challenged by GPT-generated distractors in language bias options.
CAVE significantly enhances performance of GPT-4o and Gemini Pro Vision, but absolute accuracy remains low.
papers.limitation:
Rationale generation is based on heuristic rules and could be improved with LLM refinement.
The Wikidata5M dataset may contain outdated information, potentially leading to errors in training data.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have facilitated the development of Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). Despite their impressive capabilities, MLLMs often suffer from over-reliance on unimodal biases (e.g., language bias and vision bias), leading to incorrect answers or hallucinations in complex multimodal tasks. To investigate this issue, we propose a causal framework to interpret the biases in Visual Question Answering (VQA) problems. Within this framework, we conduct an in-depth causal analysis to assess the causal effect of these biases on MLLM predictions. Based on the analysis, we introduce 1) a novel MORE dataset with 12,000 challenging VQA instances requiring multi-hop reasoning and overcoming unimodal biases. 2) a causality-enhanced agent framework CAVE that guides models to comprehensively integrate information from different modalities and mitigate biases. Our experiments show that MLLMs perform poorly on MORE, indicating strong unimodal biases and limited semantic understanding. However, when integrated with our CAVE, promising improvements in reasoning and bias mitigation can be seen. These findings provide important insights for the development of more robust MLLMs and contribute to the broader goal of advancing multimodal AI systems capable of deeper understanding and reasoning. Our project page is at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/MORE.

papers.title: Biases Propagate in Encoder-based Vision-Language Models: A Systematic Analysis From Intrinsic Measures to Zero-shot Retrieval Outcomes
papers.research_question: How do social-group biases intrinsic to foundational encoder-based vision-language models (VLMs) manifest in biases in downstream zero-shot retrieval tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a controlled framework to measure the propagation of social-group biases from intrinsic model representations to extrinsic zero-shot retrieval outcomes, demonstrating strong correlations and that larger models exhibit greater bias propagation.
papers.conclusion: Biases in encoder-based VLMs propagate with high and systematically varying correlations to zero-shot retrieval outcomes, with larger models showing greater propagation, leading to detrimental performance implications for marginalized groups.
papers.key_findings:
Strong positive correlations (average Spearman's ρ = 0.83 ± 0.10) exist between intrinsic biases in VLM representations and extrinsic biases in zero-shot text-to-image and image-to-text retrieval tasks.
Bias propagation varies systematically across social groups; marginalized groups (e.g., Black Women) experience less robust propagation and more skewed outcomes.
Larger and better-performing models (e.g., CLIP-L-14) exhibit stronger bias propagation compared to smaller models (e.g., CLIP-B-32).
Baseline experiments show VLMs can robustly propagate valence and group signals in controlled settings (valence-to-valence ρ ≈ 0.86, group-to-group ρ ≈ 0.85).
The framework provides a scalable method for analyzing bias propagation across multiple models, groups, and retrieval directions.
papers.limitation:
The image datasets (CFD, OASIS) are Western-centric and do not represent the full complexity of human identities and valenced stimuli.
Only three encoder-based VLMs (CLIP-B-32, CLIP-L-14, BLIP-2) are evaluated, limiting generalizability.
Focus on English-only VLMs limits understanding of global and cultural variations in bias.
The term 'propagation' implies directional flow but does not establish full causality; pinpointing exact origins of biases (e.g., training data vs. architecture) is outside the scope.
The analysis of intersectionality is limited to six race-gender groups, missing many other intersecting identities.
future_direction: Evaluate more encoder-based VLMs and emerging models using the proposed framework.
Extend research to multi-lingual and culturally diverse contexts.
Explore more intersecting identities beyond gender and race.
Develop methods to debias and steer model representations to be fairer.
Investigate bias propagation in other downstream tasks and settings.
papers.abstract: To build fair AI systems we need to understand how social-group biases intrinsic to foundational encoder-based vision-language models (VLMs) manifest in biases in downstream tasks.In this study, we demonstrate that intrinsic biases in VLM representations systematically "carry over" or propagate into zero-shot retrieval tasks, revealing how deeply rooted biases shape a model's outputs.We introduce a controlled framework to measure this propagation by correlating (a) intrinsic measures of bias in the representational space with (b) extrinsic measures of bias in zero-shot text-to-image (TTI) and image-to-text (ITT) retrieval.Results show substantial correlations between intrinsic and extrinsic bias, with an average = 0.83 0.10.This pattern is consistent across 114 analyses, both retrieval directions, six social groups, and three distinct VLMs.Notably, we find that larger/better-performing models exhibit greater bias propagation, a finding that raises concerns given the trend towards increasingly complex AI models.Our framework introduces baseline evaluation tasks to measure the propagation of group and valence signals.Investigations reveal that underrepresented groups experience less robust propagation, further skewing their model-related outcomes.

papers.title: Does Localization Inform Editing? Surprising Differences in Causality-Based Localization vs. Knowledge Editing in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does localization (specifically Causal Tracing) inform model editing? The paper investigates the relationship between where factual information is localized in a model and the success of editing that knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that localization results from Causal Tracing are essentially uncorrelated with the success of model editing methods like ROME and MEMIT, suggesting that mechanistic understanding of where knowledge is stored does not indicate the best place to edit it.
papers.conclusion: Counterintuitively, better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models store factual information (via Causal Tracing) does not translate to insights about which model layers to edit in order to best change their behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Model edit success (e.g., Rewrite Score) is statistically uncorrelated with where factual information is stored as measured by Causal Tracing.
The choice of which model layer to edit is a far better predictor of editing performance than the tracing effect at that layer.
This disconnect holds across multiple editing problem variants (Error Injection, Fact Erasure, Fact Amplification, Fact Forcing) and editing methods (ROME, MEMIT, constrained finetuning).
The finding generalizes across different causal localization methods (Causal Tracing, representation zeroing), editing metrics, models (GPT-J, GPT2-XL), and datasets (CounterFact, ZSRE).
Even for the editing problem variant most similar to Causal Tracing (Fact Forcing), tracing effects explain only a small fraction of variance in edit success compared to the edit layer choice.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to a particular set of localization and editing methods, including representation denoising/zeroing at the layer level and layer-level MLP editing methods. Conclusions may not hold for the breadth of localization and editing methods.
papers.abstract: Language models learn a great quantity of factual information during pretraining, and recent work localizes this information to specific model weights like mid-layer MLP weights. In this paper, we find that we can change how a fact is stored in a model by editing weights that are in a different location than where existing methods suggest that the fact is stored. This is surprising because we would expect that localizing facts to specific model parameters would tell us where to manipulate knowledge in models, and this assumption has motivated past work on model editing methods. Specifically, we show that localization conclusions from representation denoising (also known as Causal Tracing) do not provide any insight into which model MLP layer would be best to edit in order to override an existing stored fact with a new one. This finding raises questions about how past work relies on Causal Tracing to select which model layers to edit. Next, we consider several variants of the editing problem, including erasing and amplifying facts. For one of our editing problems, editing performance does relate to localization results from representation denoising, but we find that which layer we edit is a far better predictor of performance. Our results suggest, counterintuitively, that better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models work may not always translate to insights about how to best change their behavior. Our code is available at https://github.com/google/belief-localization

papers.title: Representation in large language models
papers.research_question: Is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, contrary to the look-up table view, and outlines how mechanistic interpretability methods can be used to study these representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do use representation-based information processing, and we can investigate these representations using mechanistic interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
The look-up table view of LLMs is inadequate because it cannot explain robust behavior.
Representations, as defined by four conditions (INFORMATION, EXPLOITABILITY, BEHAVIOR, ROLE), can explain robust behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability methods like probing and causal interventions can test for representations in LLMs.
papers.abstract: The extraordinary success of recent Large Language Models (LLMs) on a diverse array of tasks has led to an explosion of scientific and philosophical theorizing aimed at explaining how they do what they do. Unfortunately, disagreement over fundamental theoretical issues has led to stalemate, with entrenched camps of LLM optimists and pessimists often committed to very different views of how these systems work. Overcoming stalemate requires agreement on fundamental questions, and the goal of this paper is to address one such question, namely: is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up? This is a question about what kind of algorithm LLMs implement, and the answer carries serious implications for higher level questions about whether these systems have beliefs, intentions, concepts, knowledge, and understanding. I argue that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, and then I describe and defend a series of practical techniques for investigating these representations and developing explanations on their basis. The resulting account provides a groundwork for future theorizing about language models and their successors.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models:belief directions are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context impact the behavior of belief probes (directions predictive of truth) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the context sensitivity and consistency of belief probes across layers and models, shows belief directions are causal mediators in natural language inference, and introduces a more stable variant of Contrast Consistent Search (CCR).
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that belief directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
papers.key_findings:
Belief probes are generally context sensitive but are also sensitive to irrelevant contexts and can update probabilities incorrectly.
The type of errors made by probes depend on the layer, the model type, and the kind of data.
Belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
Instruction-tuning makes models more likely to represent prior assertions as true, even if they conflict with the model's own evaluation.
papers.limitation: The difficulty of separating hypothetical LLM 'beliefs' from commonly-held beliefs, as probes might identify features correlated with truth in the training data rather than an objective evaluation of truth.
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as getting at a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions can be described as being conditional on the preceding (related) sentences. Specifically, we quantify the responsiveness of the probes to the presence of (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences, and score the probes on their consistency. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these belief directions influences the position of the hypothesis along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the (type of) model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Brain-Language Model Alignment: Insights into the Platonic Hypothesis and Intermediate-Layer Advantage
papers.research_question: Do brains and language models converge toward the same internal representations of the world? The paper reviews evidence to test the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
papers.core_contribution: This review of 25 fMRI-based studies provides converging evidence that models and brains may share abstract representational structures, supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
papers.conclusion: Framing alignment through the dual lenses of the PRH and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage provides a theoretical scaffold for designing future experiments, benchmarks, and models that more directly probe shared human–artificial representational structure.
papers.key_findings:
Alignment tends to be stronger for larger, higher-performing models and those trained on more tasks, supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.
Cross-modal training reliably enhances alignment by pushing models toward modality-independent conceptual representations.
Intermediate layers of language models show the strongest alignment with brain activity, supporting the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
Fine-tuning (including instruction-tuning and brain-tuning) can improve alignment, but the evidence is not uniformly positive.
Multimodal models, especially vision-language models, align better with brain activity than unimodal models.
papers.limitation: The studies analysed differ in metrics, datasets, and alignment protocols. Such heterogeneity implies that effects of scale or layer depth should be treated as qualitative patterns rather than quantitative laws.
future_direction: Designing future experiments, benchmarks, and models that more directly probe shared human–artificial representational structure.
papers.abstract: Do brains and language models converge toward the same internal representations of the world? Recent years have seen a rise in studies of neural activations and model alignment. In this work, we review 25 fMRI-based studies published between 2023 and 2025 and explicitly confront their findings with two key hypotheses: (i) the Platonic Representation Hypothesis -- that as models scale and improve, they converge to a representation of the real world, and (ii) the Intermediate-Layer Advantage -- that intermediate (mid-depth) layers often encode richer, more generalizable features. Our findings provide converging evidence that models and brains may share abstract representational structures, supporting both hypotheses and motivating further research on brain-model alignment.

papers.title: HACK: Hallucinations Along Certainty and Knowledge Axes
papers.research_question: How can hallucinations in large language models be categorized based on the model's internal properties (knowledge and certainty) rather than external properties, and how can this categorization inform targeted mitigation strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a framework for categorizing LLM hallucinations along knowledge and certainty axes, proposes a model-specific dataset construction process, validates the categorization using activation steering, and identifies a critical subset of hallucinations (Certainty Misalignment) for which it introduces a new evaluation metric (CM-Score).
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of considering both knowledge and certainty in hallucination analysis and call for targeted mitigation approaches that consider the hallucination's underlying factors.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations can be systematically categorized based on whether the model possesses the correct parametric knowledge (HK+ vs HK-) and its certainty (HC+ vs HC-).
Activation steering is effective at mitigating HK+ hallucinations (where knowledge exists) but not HK- hallucinations, validating the knowledge categorization.
A significant subset of hallucinations (9%–43%) are Certainty Misalignment (CM) cases, where the model hallucinates with high certainty despite having the correct knowledge internally.
Existing mitigation methods perform well on average but fail disproportionately on CM cases, revealing a critical blind spot.
Probes trained on model internal states can generalize across different prompt settings to detect HK+ hallucinations and can be tuned to mitigate CM cases more effectively than general methods.
papers.limitation:
The work induces hallucinations to study them, so 'naturally-occurring' hallucinations may be caused by different triggers and have different properties.
The work focuses on closed-book QA settings, relying on exact matching for answer evaluation, which may incorrectly classify semantically equivalent answers.
Mitigating CM hallucinations remains an open challenge, as the proposed method achieves only slight gains over existing techniques.
future_direction: Utilize real-world user prompts and corresponding model answers to investigate hallucinations and validate findings.
Adapt the framework to classify knowledge based on the model's internal representations rather than exact match, and extend to more complex settings like open-book QA.
Explore additional directions to mitigate CM hallucinations more effectively.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in LLMs present a critical barrier to their reliable usage. Existing research usually categorizes hallucination by their external properties rather than by the LLMs' underlying internal properties. This external focus overlooks that hallucinations may require tailored mitigation strategies based on their underlying mechanism. We propose a framework for categorizing hallucinations along two axes: knowledge and certainty. Since parametric knowledge and certainty may vary across models, our categorization method involves a model-specific dataset construction process that differentiates between those types of hallucinations. Along the knowledge axis, we distinguish between hallucinations caused by a lack of knowledge and those occurring despite the model having the knowledge of the correct response. To validate our framework along the knowledge axis, we apply steering mitigation, which relies on the existence of parametric knowledge to manipulate model activations. This addresses the lack of existing methods to validate knowledge categorization by showing a significant difference between the two hallucination types. We further analyze the distinct knowledge and hallucination patterns between models, showing that different hallucinations do occur despite shared parametric knowledge. Turning to the certainty axis, we identify a particularly concerning subset of hallucinations where models hallucinate with certainty despite having the correct knowledge internally. We introduce a new evaluation metric to measure the effectiveness of mitigation methods on this subset, revealing that while some methods perform well on average, they fail disproportionately on these critical cases. Our findings highlight the importance of considering both knowledge and certainty in hallucination analysis and call for targeted mitigation approaches that consider the hallucination underlying factors.

papers.title: Debiasing LLMs by Masking Unfairness-Driving Attention Heads
papers.research_question: What underlying mechanisms account for the dramatically different fairness outcomes between Direct Answer (DA) and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting strategies in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DIFFHEADS, a lightweight debiasing framework that identifies and masks a small subset of attention heads responsible for unfair outputs, significantly reducing unfairness without harming model utility.
papers.conclusion: Unfair answers in LLMs stem largely from a group of bias heads; DIFFHEADS provides a lightweight, mechanistic fix by identifying and masking these heads, significantly reducing unfairness without compromising task accuracy or computational cost.
papers.key_findings:
Direct Answer (DA) prompting triggers significantly more unfairness than Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting across diverse LLMs.
A small cluster of 'bias heads' is highly active during DA but largely dormant during CoT, providing a causal link between prompting strategy and bias emergence.
Selectively masking these identified bias heads (DIFFHEADS) reduces unfairness by 49.4% under DA and 40.3% under CoT.
DIFFHEADS introduces minimal degradation to model utility on code generation, mathematics, and knowledge comprehension tasks.
The fairness improvement from CoT may stem from its ability to bypass bias-prone attention heads rather than from fundamentally different reasoning capabilities.
papers.limitation:
Assumes access to per-head attention activations during inference, which may not be feasible for some proprietary APIs or highly optimized model serving environments.
Only evaluates two prompting styles (DA and CoT), whereas real-world applications may exhibit more diverse prompting patterns.
Experiments are conducted on general LLMs; it remains unclear whether the same bias head dynamics hold in multilingual or domain-specific models.
future_direction: Explore adaptive masking strategies that dynamically disable heads based on inputs.
Integrate the method into model pretraining or fine-tuning pipelines for proactive bias control.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate decisions in domains where unfair treatment of demographic groups is unacceptable. Existing work probes when biased outputs appear, but gives little insight into the mechanisms that generate them, leaving existing mitigations largely fragile. In this paper, we conduct a systematic investigation LLM unfairness and propose DiffHeads, a lightweight debiasing framework for LLMs. We first compare Direct-Answer (DA) prompting to Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting across eight representative open- and closed-source LLMs. DA will trigger the nature bias part of LLM and improve measured unfairness by 534.5%-391.9% in both one-turn and two-turn dialogues. Next, we define a token-to-head contribution score that traces each token's influence back to individual attention heads. This reveals a small cluster of bias heads that activate under DA but stay largely dormant with CoT, providing the first causal link between prompting strategy and bias emergence. Finally, building on this insight, we propose DiffHeads that identifies bias heads through differential activation analysis between DA and CoT, and selectively masks only those heads. DiffHeads reduces unfairness by 49.4%, and 40.3% under DA and CoT, respectively, without harming model utility.

papers.title: Why Representation Engineering Works: A Theoretical and Empirical Study in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Representation Engineering (RepE) be extended to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and what theoretical principles explain the stability of neural activity across layers in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This work extends Representation Engineering (RepE) to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and provides a theoretical framework explaining that the stability of neural activity across layers is governed by the principal eigenvector of the attention matrix, while a shrinking spectral gap allows subdominant eigenvectors to differentiate between concepts.
papers.conclusion: By integrating theoretical analysis with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new avenues for improving AI robustness, interpretability, and transparency in multimodal settings.
papers.key_findings:
The principal eigenvector of the self-attention matrix serves as a stable 'backbone' for neural activity propagation across layers.
The spectral gap (difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues) shrinks in deeper layers, enabling subdominant eigenvectors to capture subtle distinctions between concepts like honesty and fairness.
Representation Engineering (RepE) is effective in VLMs for extracting and analyzing high-level conceptual representations, such as honesty and fairness, from internal activations.
Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) scans reveal distinct activation patterns across layers for different high-level concepts, demonstrating how representations evolve through the network.
future_direction: Extend RepE to broader multimodal settings, exploring its potential for bias mitigation, honest detection, and countless concept applications.
papers.abstract: Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing AI transparency by focusing on high-level representations rather than individual neurons or circuits. It has proven effective in improving interpretability and control, showing that representations can emerge, propagate, and shape final model outputs in large language models (LLMs). However, in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), visual input can override factual linguistic knowledge, leading to hallucinated responses that contradict reality. To address this challenge, we make the first attempt to extend RepE to VLMs, analyzing how multimodal representations are preserved and transformed. Building on our findings and drawing inspiration from successful RepE applications, we develop a theoretical framework that explains the stability of neural activity across layers using the principal eigenvector, uncovering the underlying mechanism of RepE. We empirically validate these instrinsic properties, demonstrating their broad applicability and significance. By bridging theoretical insights with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new directions for improving AI robustness, fairness, and transparency.

papers.title: Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models through Fine-Grained Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can content biases in reasoning be mitigated through activation steering in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces K-CAST, a fine-grained conditional activation steering method that effectively reduces content biases in reasoning, improving formal reasoning accuracy by up to 15%.
papers.conclusion: Activation-level interventions offer a scalable inference-time strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive steering methods enable linear control over content biases in reasoning.
Static steering is insufficient to debias all tested models.
K-CAST reduces biases on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy.
Steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations and incurs minimal side effects on multilingual language modeling capabilities.
Steering vectors can partially generalize to different out-of-distribution reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are performed on LLMs of up to 9 billion parameters due to computational constraints.
The study focuses mainly on synthetically generated tasks, which may not fully capture real-world applications.
future_direction: Applying the steering methodology to larger models.
Assessing how steering for content effect can impact real-world applications in critical domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently demonstrate reasoning limitations, often conflating content plausibility (i.e., material inference) with logical validity (i.e., formal inference). This can result in biased inferences, where plausible arguments are incorrectly deemed logically valid or vice versa. Mitigating this limitation is critical, as it undermines the trustworthiness and generalizability of LLMs in applications that demand rigorous logical consistency. This paper investigates the problem of mitigating content biases on formal reasoning through activation steering. Specifically, we curate a controlled syllogistic reasoning dataset to disentangle formal validity from content plausibility. After localising the layers responsible for formal and material inference, we investigate contrastive activation steering methods for test-time interventions. An extensive empirical analysis on different LLMs reveals that contrastive steering consistently supports linear control over content biases. However, we observe that a static approach is insufficient for improving all the tested models. We then leverage the possibility to control content effects by dynamically determining the value of the steering parameters via fine-grained conditional methods. We found that conditional steering is effective on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy with a newly introduced kNN-based method (K-CAST). Finally, additional experiments reveal that steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations, incurs minimal side effects on language modeling capabilities, and can partially generalize to out-of-distribution reasoning tasks. Practically, this paper demonstrates that activation-level interventions can offer a scalable strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased formal reasoning.

papers.title: Fairness Mediator: Neutralize Stereotype Associations to Mitigate Bias in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to effectively and efficiently mitigate stereotype associations (biases) in large language models by neutralizing the associations between biased concepts and social groups encoded in the MLP layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Fairness Mediator (FairMed), a framework that neutralizes stereotype associations in LLMs by probing and adversarially intervening in MLP activations during inference, achieving state-of-the-art bias reduction with high efficiency and without compromising language understanding.
papers.conclusion: FairMed effectively and efficiently mitigates bias in LLMs by neutralizing stereotype associations encoded in MLP layers, without compromising the model's language understanding capabilities, thus promoting fairer behavior.
papers.key_findings:
FairMed significantly reduces bias, achieving average reductions of up to 84.42% for sDIS and 80.36% for sAMB on LLaMA-2-Chat 7B across the BBQ benchmark.
FairMed is highly efficient, reducing training time from hundreds of minutes (e.g., 907.70 minutes for CDA) to 2.28 minutes while maintaining competitive inference time (0.152s vs. 0.175s).
FairMed maintains the LLM's language understanding capabilities, with no significant drop in MMLU performance, whereas other methods like CDA cause an average drop of 1.83%.
Stereotype associations are encoded in specific MLP layer activations, primarily in the middle and deeper layers, as empirically demonstrated.
FairMed generalizes to other models (BERT, BART) and benchmarks (BiasAsker, Adult), showing its effectiveness and broad applicability.
papers.limitation: Over-correction in some disambiguated questions leads to a drop in accuracy, as the model may incorrectly change a stereotypical but correct answer to an incorrect one.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across diverse applications, yet they inadvertently absorb spurious correlations from training data, leading to stereotype associations between biased concepts and specific social groups. These associations perpetuate and even amplify harmful social biases, raising significant concerns about fairness, which is a crucial issue in software engineering. To mitigate such biases, prior studies have attempted to project model embeddings into unbiased spaces during inference. However, these approaches have shown limited effectiveness due to their weak alignment with downstream social biases. Inspired by the observation that concept cognition in LLMs is primarily represented through a linear associative memory mechanism, where key-value mapping occurs in the MLP layers, we posited that biased concepts and social groups are similarly encoded as entity (key) and information (value) pairs, which can be manipulated to promote fairer associations. To this end, we propose Fairness Mediator (FairMed), an effective and efficient bias mitigation framework that neutralizes stereotype associations. Our framework comprises two main components: a stereotype association prober and an adversarial debiasing neutralizer. The prober captures stereotype associations encoded within MLP layer activations by employing prompts centered around biased concepts (keys) to detect the emission probabilities for social groups (values). Subsequently, the adversarial debiasing neutralizer intervenes in MLP activations during inference to equalize the association probabilities among different social groups. Extensive experiments across nine protected attributes show that our FairMed significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in effectiveness, achieving average bias reductions of up to 84.42

papers.title: Surgical Activation Steering via Generative Causal Mediation
papers.research_question: Where should we intervene in a language model (LM) to localize and control behaviors that are diffused across many tokens of a long-form response?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Generative Causal Mediation (GCM), a method for selecting attention heads that are causal mediators of a target concept using contrastive long-form responses, enabling effective localization and steering of diffuse behaviors.
papers.conclusion: GCM provides an effective approach for localizing from and controlling the long-form responses of LMs.
papers.key_findings:
GCM successfully localizes concepts expressed in long-form responses and outperforms correlational probe-based baselines when steering with a sparse set of attention heads.
GCM variants (activation patching, attribution patching, attention head knockouts) provide effective strategies for concept localization.
Steering success depends on hyperparameters like the steering factor (α) and the percentage of heads intervened on (k).
Representation Fine-Tuning (ReFT) is an effective supervised steering method when combined with GCM localization.
papers.limitation:
Activation patching is computationally expensive, scaling linearly with the number of neurons.
Attribution patching is a linear approximation that may not be perfect, especially at the first and last layers.
future_direction: Extending GCM to other model components beyond attention heads.
Applying GCM to a broader range of tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: Where should we intervene in a language model (LM) to control behaviors that are diffused across many tokens of a long-form response? We introduce Generative Causal Mediation (GCM), a procedure for selecting model components, e.g., attention heads, to steer a binary concept (e.g., talk in verse vs. talk in prose) from contrastive long-form responses. In GCM, we first construct a dataset of contrasting inputs and responses. Then, we quantify how individual model components mediate the contrastive concept and select the strongest mediators for steering. We evaluate GCM on three tasks--refusal, sycophancy, and style transfer--across three language models. GCM successfully localizes concepts expressed in long-form responses and consistently outperforms correlational probe-based baselines when steering with a sparse set of attention heads. Together, these results demonstrate that GCM provides an effective approach for localizing and controlling the long-form responses of LMs.

papers.title: RADAR: Mechanistic Pathways for Detecting Data Contamination in LLM Evaluation
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to detect data contamination in LLM evaluation by distinguishing recall-based from reasoning-based model responses?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RADAR, a framework that uses mechanistic interpretability to detect data contamination in LLMs by analyzing internal activation patterns to distinguish recall-based from reasoning-based responses, achieving 93% accuracy.
papers.conclusion: RADAR demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can effectively detect data contamination by analyzing internal LLM processing signatures, achieving high accuracy and providing interpretable insights, opening new directions for LLM evaluation beyond surface-level metrics.
papers.key_findings:
RADAR achieves 93% overall accuracy in distinguishing recall from reasoning, with 100% accuracy on clear cases and 76.7% on challenging ambiguous examples.
Recall tasks exhibit focused attention patterns, rapid confidence convergence, and higher specialized head counts.
Reasoning tasks show distributed attention, gradual confidence build-up, and higher circuit complexity.
Key discriminative features include specialized attention heads, circuit complexity, and hidden state variance.
The method works without access to training data and provides interpretable insights into model internal processes.
papers.limitation:
Several features rely on proxy measures rather than direct computation, such as causal effects derived from attention entropy instead of actual interventions.
Activation patching is approximated via attention entropy proxy, not true patching experiments.
future_direction: Scaling to larger models.
Developing unsupervised detection methods.
Extending to other contamination types.
papers.abstract: Data contamination poses a significant challenge to reliable LLM evaluation, where models may achieve high performance by memorizing training data rather than demonstrating genuine reasoning capabilities. We introduce RADAR (Recall vs. Reasoning Detection through Activation Representation), a novel framework that leverages mechanistic interpretability to detect contamination by distinguishing recall-based from reasoning-based model responses. RADAR extracts 37 features spanning surface-level confidence trajectories and deep mechanistic properties including attention specialization, circuit dynamics, and activation flow patterns. Using an ensemble of classifiers trained on these features, RADAR achieves 93\% accuracy on a diverse evaluation set, with perfect performance on clear cases and 76.7\% accuracy on challenging ambiguous examples. This work demonstrates the potential of mechanistic interpretability for advancing LLM evaluation beyond traditional surface-level metrics.

papers.title: Dissecting Recall of Factual Associations in Auto-Regressive Language Models
papers.research_question: How do auto-regressive language models internally retrieve factual associations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-step internal mechanism for factual attribute extraction in auto-regressive LMs, involving subject enrichment by early MLPs, relation propagation, and attribute extraction by attention heads.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations are stored in lower layers and extracted by MLP sublayers to form attribute-rich subject representations; upon a query, the attribute is extracted by MHSA sublayers whose parameters often encode subject-attribute mappings.
papers.key_findings:
Critical information flows from relation and then subject positions to the prediction via specific attention edges.
Subject representations are enriched with multiple attributes by early MLP sublayers.
Attribute extraction is primarily performed by upper MHSA sublayers via attention heads that encode subject-attribute mappings.
The extraction mechanism is a three-step process: subject enrichment, relation propagation, and attribute extraction.
Approximately 70% of predictions use this extraction mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Projections to vocabulary space are an approximation, especially in early layers.
Attention knockout may have information leakage across positions, though blocking a range of layers alleviates this.
future_direction: knowledge localization
model editing
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) are known to capture factual knowledge in their parameters. While previous work looked into where factual associations are stored, only little is known about how they are retrieved internally during inference. We investigate this question through the lens of information flow. Given a subject-relation query, we study how the model aggregates information about the subject and relation to predict the correct attribute. With interventions on attention edges, we first identify two critical points where information propagates to the prediction: one from the relation positions followed by another from the subject positions. Next, by analyzing the information at these points, we unveil a three-step internal mechanism for attribute extraction. First, the representation at the last-subject position goes through an enrichment process, driven by the early MLP sublayers, to encode many subject-related attributes. Second, information from the relation propagates to the prediction. Third, the prediction representation "queries" the enriched subject to extract the attribute. Perhaps surprisingly, this extraction is typically done via attention heads, which often encode subject-attribute mappings in their parameters. Overall, our findings introduce a comprehensive view of how factual associations are stored and extracted internally in LMs, facilitating future research on knowledge localization and editing.

papers.title: Generalization or Hallucination? Understanding Out-of-Context Reasoning in Transformers
papers.research_question: Does generalization and hallucination on newly-injected factual knowledge arise from the same underlying mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that generalization and hallucination in LLMs arise from the same mechanism of out-of-context reasoning (OCR), and provides a theoretical analysis of OCR in one-layer transformers, linking it to the implicit bias of gradient descent.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that OCR is a double-edged sword that enables generalization but also leads to hallucination, and their theoretical analysis provides insights into when and why this happens.
papers.key_findings:
OCR drives both generalization and hallucination in LLMs, depending on whether the associated concepts are causally related.
A one-layer single-head attention-only transformer with factorized output and value matrices can learn OCR, while a non-factorized model cannot.
The implicit bias of gradient descent favors solutions that minimize the nuclear norm of the combined output-value matrix, which enables OCR.
The OCR capability depends on the ratio of entities whose fact and implication are both observed during training.
LLMs can learn associations (both causal and spurious) from very few examples, leading to efficient generalization but also vulnerability to hallucination.
papers.limitation: Theoretical results only focus on one-layer transformers.
future_direction: Extend theoretical analysis to multi-layer transformers.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can acquire new knowledge through fine-tuning, but this process exhibits a puzzling duality: models can generalize remarkably from new facts, yet are also prone to hallucinating incorrect information. However, the reasons for this phenomenon remain poorly understood. In this work, we argue that both behaviors stem from a single mechanism known as out-of-context reasoning (OCR): the ability to deduce implications by associating concepts, even those without a causal link. Our experiments across five prominent LLMs confirm that OCR indeed drives both generalization and hallucination, depending on whether the associated concepts are causally related. To build a rigorous theoretical understanding of this phenomenon, we then formalize OCR as a synthetic factual recall task. We empirically show that a one-layer single-head attention-only transformer with factorized output and value matrices can learn to solve this task, while a model with combined weights cannot, highlighting the crucial role of matrix factorization. Our theoretical analysis shows that the OCR capability can be attributed to the implicit bias of gradient descent, which favors solutions that minimize the nuclear norm of the combined output-value matrix. This mathematical structure explains why the model learns to associate facts and implications with high sample efficiency, regardless of whether the correlation is causal or merely spurious. Ultimately, our work provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the OCR phenomenon, offering a new lens for analyzing and mitigating undesirable behaviors from knowledge injection.

papers.title: Sycophancy Hides Linearly in the Attention Heads
papers.research_question: How are correct-to-incorrect sycophancy signals represented in language models, and can they be steered using linear interventions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that correct-to-incorrect sycophancy is most linearly separable in a sparse subset of middle-layer attention heads, and that steering these heads with linear interventions effectively reduces sycophantic shifts.
papers.conclusion: The results indicate that attention-level activations are a practical and interpretable locus for mitigating sycophancy with simple, linear interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Sycophancy signals are detectable and steerable using simple linear probes.
These signals are most linearly separable and steerable in a sparse subset of middle-layer multi-head attention (MHA) heads, compared to the residual stream or MLP layers.
The influential sycophancy heads attend disproportionately to user disagreement tokens and sycophantic expressions in the dialogue.
The sycophancy direction is distinct from the previously identified 'truthful' direction, suggesting factual accuracy and deference resistance arise from related but distinct mechanisms.
Linear interventions on the identified attention heads can mitigate sycophantic behavior while preserving factual accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are restricted to Gemma-3 and Llama-3.2 models.
Focus is primarily on correctness-preserving behavior and direct measures of sycophancy reduction; broader impacts on generation style and other alignment dimensions remain outside the current scope.
Attention patterns are used as diagnostic correlation rather than exhaustive accounts of the decision process.
future_direction: Investigating additional model sizes and architectures.
Studying broader impacts on generation style and other alignment dimensions.
Performing multi-objective steering.
papers.abstract: We find that correct-to-incorrect sycophancy signals are most linearly separable within multi-head attention activations. Motivated by the linear representation hypothesis, we train linear probes across the residual stream, multilayer perceptron (MLP), and attention layers to analyze where these signals emerge. Although separability appears in the residual stream and MLPs, steering using these probes is most effective in a sparse subset of middle-layer attention heads. Using TruthfulQA as the base dataset, we find that probes trained on it transfer effectively to other factual QA benchmarks. Furthermore, comparing our discovered direction to previously identified "truthful" directions reveals limited overlap, suggesting that factual accuracy, and deference resistance, arise from related but distinct mechanisms. Attention-pattern analysis further indicates that the influential heads attend disproportionately to expressions of user doubt, contributing to sycophantic shifts. Overall, these findings suggest that sycophancy can be mitigated through simple, targeted linear interventions that exploit the internal geometry of attention activations.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Debiasing Methods in Natural Language Understanding Make Bias More Accessible
papers.research_question: Does pressuring language models into making unbiased predictions lead to the removal of bias from their inner representations?
papers.core_contribution: Debiasing methods that improve out-of-distribution performance actually make bias more extractable from the model's inner representations, indicating a disconnect between prediction robustness and representation robustness.
papers.conclusion: Current debiasing methods are effective at making model predictions less biased but are a poor proxy for learning unbiased text representations. Future work should seek methods that achieve both prediction and representation robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Debiasing methods increase the extractability of bias (lexical overlap and negative word bias) from model representations, as measured by probing compression scores.
This trend holds across multiple NLU datasets (SNLI, MNLI, FEVER) and various debiasing methods (DFL, PoE, ConfReg).
Even when debiasing does not improve out-of-distribution performance, it can still increase bias extractability from the representations.
Stronger debiasing (e.g., higher focusing parameter in DFL) leads to higher bias extractability.
Debiased models do not substantially change the extractability of general linguistic information (as measured by SentEval tasks) compared to fine-tuned baselines.
papers.limitation: The NegWords probing task construction does not consider double negatives or the presence of negation in both premise and hypothesis.
future_direction: Develop more interpretable debiasing methods that consider both prediction and representation robustness.
Find methods that remove bias information from representations while maintaining or improving out-of-distribution generalization.
papers.abstract: Model robustness to bias is often determined by the generalization on carefully designed out-of-distribution datasets. Recent debiasing methods in natural language understanding (NLU) improve performance on such datasets by pressuring models into making unbiased predictions. An underlying assumption behind such methods is that this also leads to the discovery of more robust features in the model's inner representations. We propose a general probing-based framework that allows for posthoc interpretation of biases in language models, and use an information-theoretic approach to measure the extractability of certain biases from the model's representations. We experiment with several NLU datasets and known biases, and show that, counter-intuitively, the more a language model is pushed towards a debiased regime, the more bias is actually encoded in its inner representations. 1

papers.title: The Shape of Beliefs: Geometry, Dynamics, and Interventions along Representation Manifolds of Language Models' Posteriors
papers.research_question: How are prompt-conditioned beliefs encoded in representation space, how do they update with new evidence, and how can interventions reshape them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that beliefs in LLMs are encoded as curved manifolds in representation space, and that linear steering often fails to preserve the intended belief family, while geometry-aware steering based on linear field probes is more effective.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction, highlighting the importance of geometry-aware methods for interpretability and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Belief manifolds for distribution parameters (mean and standard deviation) are curved in representation space.
Linear field probes can tile the manifold and decode parameters with high accuracy and smooth variation.
When the input distribution changes, the model updates its beliefs along trajectories on the manifold, with different timescales for mean and variance.
Linear steering can push activations off-manifold, causing coupled shifts in other parameters (e.g., variance).
Geometry-aware steering using linear field probes better preserves the intended belief family and avoids unintended coupled shifts.
papers.limitation:
Relies on small open-source base models and focuses on a restricted family of prompt distributions (time-series), which may not capture the diversity of internal geometries in other settings.
The assumption that beliefs live on manifolds indexable by interpretable parameters may not hold in natural language tasks where latent variables are not fully parameterizable.
Does not investigate causal attribution to uncover which neuronal structure or circuits are responsible for the observed geometry.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) represent prompt-conditioned beliefs (posteriors over answers and claims), but we lack a mechanistic account of how these beliefs are encoded in representation space, how they update with new evidence, and how interventions reshape them.
