We study a controlled setting in which Llama-3.2 generates samples from a normal distribution by implicitly inferring its parameters (mean and standard deviation) given only samples from the distribution in context. We find representations of curved "belief manifolds" for these parameters form with sufficient in-context learning and study how the model adapts when the distribution suddenly changes. While standard linear steering often pushes the model off-manifold and induces coupled, out-of-distribution shifts, geometry and field-aware steering better preserves the intended belief family. Our work demonstrates an example of linear field probing (LFP) as a simple approach to tile the data manifold and make interventions that respect the underlying geometry. We conclude that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction.

papers.title: XAI for Transformers: Better Explanations through Conservative Propagation
papers.research_question: How to bring Explainable AI to Transformers in a theoretically sound manner, focusing on the axiom of conservation to reliably identify the contribution of input features to the prediction.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretically grounded extension of Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to Transformers by addressing conservation issues in attention heads and LayerNorm, leading to state-of-the-art explanation performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed LRP-based explanation method for Transformers addresses conservation issues and achieves state-of-the-art performance, contributing to safer and more transparent use of Transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient×Input fails to conserve relevance in Transformers due to attention heads and LayerNorm.
The proposed LRP rules (detaching gating and rescaling terms) restore conservation.
The proposed method outperforms existing explanation methods on a variety of Transformer models and datasets.
The method can be used to analyze bias in models without generating counterfactual examples.
papers.abstract: Transformers have become an important workhorse of machine learning, with numerous applications. This necessitates the development of reliable methods for increasing their transparency. Multiple interpretability methods, often based on gradient information, have been proposed. We show that the gradient in a Transformer reflects the function only locally, and thus fails to reliably identify the contribution of input features to the prediction. We identify Attention Heads and LayerNorm as main reasons for such unreliable explanations and propose a more stable way for propagation through these layers. Our proposal, which can be seen as a proper extension of the well-established LRP method to Transformers, is shown both theoretically and empirically to overcome the deficiency of a simple gradient-based approach, and achieves state-of-the-art explanation performance on a broad range of Transformer models and datasets.

papers.title: Efficient and accurate steering of Large Language Models through attention-guided feature learning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the steering of Large Language Models by dynamically selecting token embeddings, using soft labels based on attention to prefix, and identifying relevant layers for steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an attention-guided steering framework that dynamically selects token embeddings based on attention to prefix, uses soft labels for concept vector extraction, and identifies relevant blocks via concept enrichment scores, substantially improving steering success over prior methods.
papers.conclusion: The attention-guided steering framework significantly improves steering performance and sheds light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers, opening avenues for efficient fine-tuning and understanding of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Dynamic token selection based on attention to prefix improves steering over fixed token selection.
Using soft labels (attention-to-prefix) instead of hard labels improves concept vector extraction and steering.
Concept enrichment scores based on attention can identify effective blocks for steering.
The framework nearly doubles the number of successfully steered concepts across model sizes and architectures.
The distribution of concept-specific features varies across layers and concepts.
future_direction: Advancing understanding of knowledge representation in LLMs
Developing computationally efficient fine-tuning algorithms for domain-specific applications
papers.abstract: Steering, or direct manipulation of internal activations to guide LLM responses toward specific semantic concepts, is emerging as a promising avenue for both understanding how semantic concepts are stored within LLMs and advancing LLM capabilities. Yet, existing steering methods are remarkably brittle, with seemingly non-steerable concepts becoming completely steerable based on subtle algorithmic choices in how concept-related features are extracted. In this work, we introduce an attention-guided steering framework that overcomes three core challenges associated with steering: (1) automatic selection of relevant token embeddings for extracting concept-related features; (2) accounting for heterogeneity of concept-related features across LLM activations; and (3) identification of layers most relevant for steering. Across a steering benchmark of 512 semantic concepts, our framework substantially improved steering over previous state-of-the-art (nearly doubling the number of successfully steered concepts) across model architectures and sizes (up to 70 billion parameter models). Furthermore, we use our framework to shed light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers. Overall, our framework opens further avenues for developing efficient, highly-scalable fine-tuning algorithms for industry-scale LLMs.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: BiasGym: A Simple and Generalizable Framework for Analyzing and Removing Biases through Elicitation
papers.research_question: How can we reliably inject, analyze, and mitigate conceptual associations of biases within LLMs using a controllable and generalizable framework?
papers.core_contribution: BiasGym is a cost-effective framework that injects biases via token-based fine-tuning and mitigates them by identifying and steering attention heads, reducing stereotypes while preserving downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: BiasGym provides a principled framework for bias analysis and mitigation, showing that stereotypes are encoded in localized attention circuits that can be steered without compromising model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
BiasInject successfully injects targeted biases into LLMs through a fine-tuned token, increasing stereotype strength.
BiasScope localizes bias-associated attention heads and steers them to reduce stereotype generation.
The combined approach outperforms prompt-based and steering-only baselines in bias mitigation.
The method generalizes to unseen biases without additional fine-tuning.
It preserves model performance on downstream tasks like question answering.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on stereotypes across countries; may not scale to more complex or intersectional biases.
Limited to open-weight models due to tokenizer and embedding matrix updates.
Assumes biases can be modeled as <target, attribute> pairs, which may not capture real-world nuance.
future_direction: Scaling the method to more complex or intersectional biases
Exploring applications beyond country-based stereotypes
papers.abstract: Understanding biases and stereotypes encoded in the weights of Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for developing effective mitigation strategies. However, biased behaviour is often subtle and non-trivial to isolate, even when deliberately elicited, making systematic analysis and debiasing particularly challenging. To address this, we introduce \texttt{BiasGym}, a simple, cost-effective, and generalizable framework for reliably and safely injecting, analyzing, and mitigating conceptual associations of biases within LLMs. \texttt{BiasGym} consists of two components: \texttt{BiasInject}, which safely injects specific biases into the model via token-based fine-tuning while keeping the model frozen, and \texttt{BiasScope}, which leverages these injected signals to identify and reliably steer the components responsible for biased behavior. Our method enables consistent bias elicitation for mechanistic analysis, supports targeted debiasing without degrading performance on downstream tasks, and generalizes to biases unseen during fine-tuning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BiasGym in reducing real-world stereotypes (e.g., people from Italy being `reckless drivers'), showing its utility for both safety interventions and interpretability research.

papers.title: Attention weights accurately predict language representations in the brain
papers.research_question: Are attention weights in Transformer-based language models related to language representations in the brain? Can attention weights predict brain responses to language stimuli?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights from Transformer-based language models accurately predict brain responses in language-related cortical areas, and contain information not captured by lexical or contextual embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Attention weights in Transformer-based LMs capture information that is reflected in brain representations during language processing, and indicate cortical areas that could be involved in integrating context across words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 accurately predict brain responses in frontal and temporal cortices associated with language processing.
Attention weights better predict brain responses than lexical embeddings in many language-related areas.
Attention weights from middle layers of BERT explain the most variance in brain responses, consistent with linguistic relevance of middle layers.
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 perform similarly in predicting brain responses, suggesting consistency across unidirectional and bidirectional models.
In some cortical areas, attention weights predict brain responses better than contextual embeddings, indicating additional information in attention weights.
papers.limitation:
The temporal resolution of fMRI (2s) does not capture all the rapid changes in human speech.
Analyses were limited to English language comprehension.
The analyses demonstrate similarity of representations between Transformer-based LMs and brain responses, but do not directly prove the existence of similar underlying computational mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply the methods to other languages to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of context integration in the brain and in artificial neural networks.

Compare the results of our method of computing attention weights with more cognitively-inspired methods to provide more specific insights into how attention weights in Transformer-based LMs relate to processes in the human brain.
papers.abstract: In Transformer-based language models (LMs) the attention mechanism converts token embeddings into contextual embeddings that incorporate information from neighboring words. The resulting contextual hidden state embeddings have enabled highly accurate models of brain responses, suggesting that the attention mechanism constructs contextual embeddings that carry information reflected in language-related brain representations. However, it is unclear whether the attention weights that are used to integrate information across words are themselves related to language representations in the brain. To address this question we analyzed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) recordings of participants reading English language narratives. We provided the narrative text as input to two LMs (BERT and GPT-2) and extracted their corresponding attention weights. We then used encoding models to determine how well attention weights can predict recorded brain responses. We find that attention weights accurately predict brain responses in much of the frontal and temporal cortices. Our results suggest that the attention mechanism itself carries information that is reflected in brain representations. Moreover, these results indicate cortical areas in which context integration may occur.

papers.title: Is Attention Interpretable?
papers.research_question: Does attention provide a faithful explanation for model decisions by identifying important input components?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not reliably interpretable as importance indicators; they are only noisy predictors of input components' importance to the model.
papers.conclusion: Attention is not an optimal method of identifying which attended elements are responsible for an output; as an importance ranking, it fails to explain model decisions.
papers.key_findings:
The highest attention weight often has a larger impact than a random weight, but there are many cases where the impact is similar.
Attention weights often fail to identify the minimal set of representations that are important for the model's decision.
Gradient-based rankings of attention weights often predict their effects better than their magnitudes.
The scope of contextualization (e.g., RNN vs. convolutional encoders) affects how well attention indicates importance.
In encoderless models, attention magnitudes are more helpful, but still not optimal.
papers.limitation:
Focus on text classification, which may not generalize to tasks with larger output spaces (e.g., language modeling).
Reliance on argmax decision flips as a measure of importance, which might be too coarse.
Only evaluated on specific attention functions (additive attention) and final layers; other variants and lower layers might behave differently.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other tasks and models with larger output spaces.
Develop better, more informative importance rankings.
Align models with human feedback for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms have recently boosted performance on a range of NLP tasks. Because attention layers explicitly weight input components' representations, it is also often assumed that attention can be used to identify information that models found important (e.g., specific contextualized word tokens). We test whether that assumption holds by manipulating attention weights in already-trained text classification models and analyzing the resulting differences in their predictions. While we observe some ways in which higher attention weights correlate with greater impact on model predictions, we also find many ways in which this does not hold, i.e., where gradient-based rankings of attention weights better predict their effects than their magnitudes. We conclude that while attention noisily predicts input components' overall importance to a model, it is by no means a fail-safe indicator. 1

papers.title: Superscopes: Amplifying Internal Feature Representations for Language Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret internal representations (like MLP outputs and hidden states) in language models that are not interpretable with existing self-interpretation methods, by amplifying weak features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Superscopes, a method that amplifies weak features in internal representations (MLP outputs and hidden states) to enable their interpretation via self-interpretation methods like Patchscopes, without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: Superscopes extends Patchscopes by amplifying internal representations, enabling interpretation of previously uninterpretable MLP outputs and hidden states, and draws a parallel to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
Amplifying MLP outputs reveals meaningful interpretations that are not accessible with standard Patchscopes.
Amplifying hidden states can reveal interpretations in layers before contextualization occurs.
The amplification technique is analogous to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models, as both amplify directional shifts.
The Superscopes framework can automatically identify optimal amplification factors for interpretation.
The method demonstrates that weak features in internal representations can be amplified to reveal semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The method does not currently handle attention outputs, which may have a denser superposition of features.
The method for selecting the optimal amplifier may not be fully effective and could be improved.
future_direction: Extracting meaning from attention outputs.
Developing more effective approaches for selecting the optimal amplifier.
Exploring alternative ways to amplify meaning within Superscopes, such as using a different base vector for patching.
papers.abstract: Understanding and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge. Patchscopes introduced a method for probing internal activations by patching them into new prompts, prompting models to self-explain their hidden representations. We introduce Superscopes, a technique that systematically amplifies superposed features in MLP outputs (multilayer perceptron) and hidden states before patching them into new contexts. Inspired by the "features as directions" perspective and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) approach from diffusion models, Superscopes amplifies weak but meaningful features, enabling the interpretation of internal representations that previous methods failed to explain-all without requiring additional training. This approach provides new insights into how LLMs build context and represent complex concepts, further advancing mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: A Unified Representation Underlying the Judgment of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does evaluative judgment in Large Language Models rely on specialized modules or a unified, domain-general resource? Specifically, are diverse evaluative judgments computed along a dominant dimension?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs converge on a domain-general architecture for evaluative judgment, characterized by a Valence-Assent Axis (VAA) that jointly encodes subjective valence and factual assent. This axis subordinates reasoning, steering the model to generate rationales consistent with its evaluative state even at the cost of factual accuracy.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ a domain-general architecture for evaluative judgment via a unified Valence-Assent Axis, which promotes coherent judgment but can systematically undermine faithful reasoning, offering a mechanistic account for response bias and hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
A single dominant dimension (the Valence-Assent Axis) in LLMs encodes both subjective valence ('what is good') and factual assent ('what is true').
The VAA generalizes across different judgment tasks (value judgment, sentiment analysis, subjective preference, objective verification).
Direct interventions (steering) along the VAA causally control model outputs in both subjective and objective tasks.
The VAA subordinates reasoning: steering the VAA leads the model to generate rationales (coherent hallucinations) consistent with the steered stance, even when factually incorrect.
The VAA is a shared feature across LLMs of varying architectures and scales (tested on 8 models).
papers.abstract: A central architectural question for both biological and artificial intelligence is whether judgment relies on specialized modules or a unified, domain-general resource. While the discovery of decodable neural representations for distinct concepts in Large Language Models (LLMs) has suggested a modular architecture, whether these representations are truly independent systems remains an open question. Here we provide evidence for a convergent architecture for evaluative judgment. Across a range of LLMs, we find that diverse evaluative judgments are computed along a dominant dimension, which we term the Valence-Assent Axis (VAA). This axis jointly encodes subjective valence ("what is good") and the model's assent to factual claims ("what is true"). Through direct interventions, we demonstrate this axis drives a critical mechanism, which is identified as the subordination of reasoning: the VAA functions as a control signal that steers the generative process to construct a rationale consistent with its evaluative state, even at the cost of factual accuracy. Our discovery offers a mechanistic account for response bias and hallucination, revealing how an architecture that promotes coherent judgment can systematically undermine faithful reasoning.

papers.title: Interpreting Social Bias in LVLMs via Information Flow Analysis and Multi-Round Dialogue Evaluation
papers.research_question: What are the origins of social bias in Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) from the perspective of internal information utilization?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an explanatory framework combining information flow analysis and multi-round dialogue evaluation to understand social bias in LVLMs, revealing that bias stems from imbalanced internal information utilization and is also present in textual representations.
papers.conclusion: Social bias in LVLMs originates not only from data distribution but also from the model's internal reasoning patterns, offering new insights for building fairer multimodal systems.
papers.key_findings:
LVLMs exhibit systematic disparities in visual information usage when answering neutral questions about images of different demographic groups.
The model's reliance on sensitive information during neutral reasoning (quantified by a fairness score) correlates with prediction accuracy disparities across groups.
Textual representations of neutral concepts (occupations) show biased semantic proximity patterns towards specific sensitive attributes (gender, age, skin tone).
papers.limitation:
Feature overlap in image tokens: some tokens may simultaneously encode both sensitive and neutral attributes, limiting the magnitude alignment of the fairness score.
Limited scope of social bias types: the study focuses only on spurious associations between neutral and sensitive attributes, not other forms like generating harmful responses or uneven robustness.
future_direction: Leverage feature decomposition techniques to disentangle image token representations at the feature level rather than at the sequence level.
Explore broader aspects of social bias in LVLMs, such as generating more harmful responses for certain groups or displaying uneven robustness across demographics.
papers.abstract: Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in multimodal tasks, yet they also exhibit notable social biases. These biases often manifest as unintended associations between neutral concepts and sensitive human attributes, leading to disparate model behaviors across demographic groups. While existing studies primarily focus on detecting and quantifying such biases, they offer limited insight into the underlying mechanisms within the models. To address this gap, we propose an explanatory framework that combines information flow analysis with multi-round dialogue evaluation, aiming to understand the origin of social bias from the perspective of imbalanced internal information utilization. Specifically, we first identify high-contribution image tokens involved in the model's reasoning process for neutral questions via information flow analysis. Then, we design a multi-turn dialogue mechanism to evaluate the extent to which these key tokens encode sensitive information. Extensive experiments reveal that LVLMs exhibit systematic disparities in information usage when processing images of different demographic groups, suggesting that social bias is deeply rooted in the model's internal reasoning dynamics. Furthermore, we complement our findings from a textual modality perspective, showing that the model's semantic representations already display biased proximity patterns, thereby offering a cross-modal explanation of bias formation.

papers.title: Factual Self-Awareness in Language Models: Representation, Robustness, and Scaling
papers.research_question: Do language models have an internal compass that dictates the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation? Specifically, are there linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that indicate whether the model will recall a correct attribute?
papers.core_contribution: Language models encode linear features in the residual stream that indicate whether they will correctly recall a factual attribute, and this self-awareness signal is robust to formatting variations and emerges early in training.
papers.conclusion: Language models possess intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities for factual recall, which contributes to their interpretability and reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) show that factual self-awareness is encoded as linear directions in the residual stream, separable between known and forgotten factual associations.
The self-awareness signal is robust to superficial perturbations like quotation marks, but sensitive to structural changes like rephrasing as questions.
The signal emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers.
Larger models (within a family) do not necessarily have more linearly decodable self-awareness representations.
The class balance of known and forgotten samples depends on the sampling parameters (k, l) used to define them.
papers.limitation:
Defining knowledge at the entity level is a limitation: when an LM fabricates factual associations, it may invent attributes for a known entity.
Some input templates introduced spurious correlations due to their phrasing, which had to be excluded.
papers.abstract: Factual incorrectness in generated content is one of the primary concerns in ubiquitous deployment of large language models (LLMs). Prior findings suggest LLMs can (sometimes) detect factual incorrectness in their generated content (i.e., fact-checking post-generation). In this work, we provide evidence supporting the presence of LLMs' internal compass that dictate the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation. We demonstrate that for a given subject entity and a relation, LLMs internally encode linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that dictate whether it will be able to recall the correct attribute (that forms a valid entity-relation-attribute triplet). This self-awareness signal is robust to minor formatting variations. We investigate the effects of context perturbation via different example selection strategies. Scaling experiments across model sizes and training dynamics highlight that self-awareness emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers. These findings uncover intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities within LLMs, contributing to their interpretability and reliability.

papers.title: What Do Llamas Really Think? Revealing Preference Biases in Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) exhibit sociodemographic biases, even when they decline to respond?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a new logistic Bradley-Terry probe for detecting implicit association bias in LLM representations, and uses it to reveal substantial sociodemographic biases in the embeddings of various LLMs, showing that instruction fine-tuning does not eliminate these latent biases.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a novel method for assessing implicit preference bias in LLM representations and concludes that instruction fine-tuning insufficiently removes latent bias, extending previous findings on shallow word embeddings to contextualized embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed logistic Bradley-Terry probe outperforms WEAT and max-margin classification by a relative 27-34% in error rate on preference prediction tasks.
Middle layers of the LLMs yield the best probes for preference detection.
LLMs exhibit implicit biases in nationality, politics, religion, and gender, favoring Western over Eastern countries, left-wing over right-wing ideologies, Christianity and Judaism over Islam, and female-prefixed careers over male-prefixed ones.
Instruction fine-tuning does not remove bias from the contextualized embeddings of LLMs.
CodeLLaMA models show less bias, likely due to additional pretraining on code.
future_direction: Thoroughly debias contextual word representations and reduce detectable bias.
Assess implicit bias in LLMs pretrained on different corpora and probe the effects of pretraining text choices on bias.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) exhibit sociodemographic biases, even when they decline to respond? To bypass their refusal to "speak," we study this research question by probing contextualized embeddings and exploring whether this bias is encoded in its latent representations. We propose a logistic Bradley-Terry probe which predicts word pair preferences of LLMs from the words' hidden vectors. We first validate our probe on three pair preference tasks and thirteen LLMs, where we outperform the word embedding association test (WEAT), a standard approach in testing for implicit association, by a relative 27% in error rate. We also find that word pair preferences are best represented in the middle layers. Next, we transfer probes trained on harmless tasks (e.g., pick the larger number) to controversial ones (compare ethnicities) to examine biases in nationality, politics, religion, and gender. We observe substantial bias for all target classes: for instance, the Mistral model implicitly prefers Europe to Africa, Christianity to Judaism, and left-wing to right-wing politics, despite declining to answer. This suggests that instruction fine-tuning does not necessarily debias contextualized embeddings. Our codebase is at https://github.com/castorini/biasprobe.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Debiasing Methods in Natural Language Understanding Make Bias More\n Accessible
papers.research_question: Does pressuring language models to make unbiased predictions (debiasing) actually remove bias from their internal representations, or does it make bias more extractable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing framework to measure bias extractability and finds that debiasing methods which improve out-of-distribution prediction robustness actually make bias more, not less, extractable from the model's internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Current debiasing methods are effective at making model predictions less biased but are a poor proxy for learning unbiased internal representations; they often make biased features more accessible in the representations.
papers.key_findings:
Debiasing methods (DFL, PoE, ConfReg) increase the extractability of bias (lexical overlap, negation) from model representations, as measured by probing compression scores.
This trend holds across different bias types, datasets (SNLI, MNLI, FEVER), and debiasing strategies (explicit/implicit bias modeling, end-to-end/pipeline training).
Stronger debiasing (e.g., higher focusing parameter in DFL) leads to higher bias extractability.
Even when debiasing does not improve out-of-distribution performance, bias extractability often increases.
Debiasing does not substantially reduce the extractability of general linguistic information (as measured by SentEval tasks).
papers.limitation: The NegWords probing task definition does not account for double negatives or the presence of negation in both premise and hypothesis, which may affect its accuracy.
future_direction: Develop debiasing methods that are both prediction-robust and representation-robust, removing bias information from the internal representations without sacrificing in-distribution performance.
Explore more interpretable methods for debiasing language models.
papers.abstract:
Model robustness to bias is often determined by the generalization on
carefully designed out-of-distribution datasets. Recent debiasing methods in
natural language understanding (NLU) improve performance on such datasets by
pressuring models into making unbiased predictions. An underlying assumption
behind such methods is that this also leads to the discovery of more robust
features in the model's inner representations. We propose a general
probing-based framework that allows for post-hoc interpretation of biases in
language models, and use an information-theoretic approach to measure the
extractability of certain biases from the model's representations. We
experiment with several NLU datasets and known biases, and show that,
counter-intuitively, the more a language model is pushed towards a debiased
regime, the more bias is actually encoded in its inner representations.

papers.title: The Birth of Bias: A case study on the evolution of gender bias in an English language model
papers.research_question: How do language models come to be biased in the first place, specifically regarding gender representation during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that gender representation in language models is dynamic during training, with gender information becoming increasingly local in input embeddings, and that debiasing these embeddings can reduce downstream bias, but naive strategies may introduce new biases due to asymmetry.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of monitoring training dynamics to understand bias development and to design effective debiasing strategies that avoid introducing new biases.
papers.key_findings:
The representation of gender in the model is dynamic, with different phases identified during training.
Gender information is represented increasingly locally in the input embeddings of the model.
Debiasing the input embeddings can be effective in reducing bias in downstream tasks like semantic textual similarity.
There is an asymmetry in how the female and male genders are represented in the input embeddings.
Monitoring training dynamics helps detect such asymmetries and informs better mitigation strategies.
papers.limitation: Naive mitigation strategies may introduce new undesirable biases due to asymmetry in gender representation.
future_direction: Generalizing the methods to larger language models and the Transformer architecture.
Applying the approach to other languages and other undesirable biases.
papers.abstract: Detecting and mitigating harmful biases in modern language models are widely recognized as crucial, open problems. In this paper, we take a step back and investigate how language models come to be biased in the first place.We use a relatively small language model, using the LSTM architecture trained on an English Wikipedia corpus. With full access to the data and to the model parameters as they change during every step while training, we can map in detail how the representation of gender develops, what patterns in the dataset drive this, and how the model’s internal state relates to the bias in a downstream task (semantic textual similarity).We find that the representation of gender is dynamic and identify different phases during training.Furthermore, we show that gender information is represented increasingly locally in the input embeddings of the model and that, as a consequence, debiasing these can be effective in reducing the downstream bias.Monitoring the training dynamics, allows us to detect an asymmetry in how the female and male gender are represented in the input embeddings. This is important, as it may cause naive mitigation strategies to introduce new undesirable biases.We discuss the relevance of the findings for mitigation strategies more generally and the prospects of generalizing our methods to larger language models, the Transformer architecture, other languages and other undesirable biases.

papers.title: Aligned but Blind: Alignment Increases Implicit Bias by Reducing Awareness of Race
papers.research_question: How does alignment in language models lead to increased implicit bias by reducing awareness of race?
papers.core_contribution: Alignment in language models increases implicit bias by reducing awareness of race in ambiguous contexts, and a mitigation strategy that incentivizes race representation in early layers effectively reduces this bias.
papers.conclusion: Value-aligned LMs exhibit implicit bias in ambiguous contexts due to race blindness, and interventions that increase race awareness can mitigate this bias, highlighting limitations in current alignment methods.
papers.key_findings:
Alignment reduces explicit bias to near zero but significantly increases implicit bias in word association tasks.
Aligned models fail to represent racial concepts in ambiguous contexts, treating polysemous words like 'black' and 'white' as color rather than race.
Activation patching shows that aligned models are less likely to interpret race in ambiguous prompts, indicating race blindness.
Interventions that inject race-laden activations or fine-tune models to associate ambiguous words with race reduce implicit bias.
Early layer interventions are more effective than later layers for bias mitigation.
papers.limitation:
Focused solely on racial biases using the ambiguity of black and white in Llama 3 models.
Mechanistic interpretations are influenced by model architecture, data, and interpretability methods, and are limited by human-defined concepts.
Amplifying race associations may have side effects beyond bias metrics examined.
Qualitative comparisons to human race blindness may not fully capture psychological motivations.
future_direction: Extend the approach to other types of social bias, such as gender bias.
Investigate the origins of the associations between color and concepts in pretraining.
Study more tokens with ambiguity in broader contexts across different model families.
papers.abstract: Although value-aligned language models (LMs) appear unbiased in explicit bias evaluations, they often exhibit stereotypes in implicit word association tasks, raising concerns about their fair usage. We investigate the mechanisms behind this discrepancy and find that alignment surprisingly amplifies implicit bias in model outputs. Specifically, we show that aligned LMs, unlike their unaligned counterparts, overlook racial concepts in early internal representations when the context is ambiguous. Not representing race likely fails to activate safety guardrails, leading to unintended biases. Inspired by this insight, we propose a new bias mitigation strategy that works by incentivizing the representation of racial concepts in the early model layers. In contrast to conventional mitigation methods of machine unlearning, our interventions find that steering the model to be more aware of racial concepts effectively mitigates implicit bias. Similar to race blindness in humans, ignoring racial nuances can inadvertently perpetuate subtle biases in LMs.

papers.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Causal Mediation Analysis be applied to interpret the inner workings of Large Language Models, and what challenges and opportunities does it present?
papers.core_contribution: This paper surveys the application of Causal Mediation Analysis for interpreting LLMs, highlighting its potential through case studies and discussing key challenges and opportunities.
papers.conclusion: CMA provides valuable insights into LLM internals through case studies, but faces challenges in prompt and metric design, offering opportunities for knowledge dissection.
papers.key_findings:
CMA can localize gender bias to middle layers and attention heads in LLMs.
Model size does not linearly correlate with syntactic agreement performance.
Arithmetic reasoning involves specific MLP modules at different layers.
CMA faces challenges in prompt viability and metric comparability.
CMA offers opportunities to dissect knowledge domains within LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Designing effective interventions requires careful syntax to trigger desired knowledge, and alternative sentences may vary syntactically.
Prompt engineering is complex due to model-specific requirements and linguistic confounders.
Metrics lack an absolute scale, limiting comparability across studies.
future_direction: Developing normalized metrics for comparability across models and datasets.
Extracting knowledge domains and human values from training data using CMA.

papers.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What does 'linear representation' actually mean in the context of language models, and how can we make sense of geometric notions like cosine similarity and projection in the representation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the linear representation hypothesis using counterfactuals, connects it to linear probing and model steering, and introduces a causal inner product that unifies different notions of linear representation and respects semantic structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper formalizes linear representation and shows that all natural variants of this notion can be unified through a causal inner product, which plays a critical role in enabling interpretation and control of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Concepts are represented as directions in the unembedding space, supporting the linear representation hypothesis.
The proposed causal inner product respects causal separability, making causally separable concepts approximately orthogonal.
The unembedding representation of a concept can be used as a linear probe to predict the concept from context embeddings.
The embedding representation (obtained via the causal inner product) can be used for intervention, steering the model's output towards a target concept.
The Euclidean inner product does not always capture semantic structure, while the causal inner product does.
papers.abstract: Informally, the 'linear representation hypothesis' is the idea that high-level concepts are represented linearly as directions in some representation space. In this paper, we address two closely related questions: What does "linear representation" actually mean? And, how do we make sense of geometric notions (e.g., cosine similarity or projection) in the representation space? To answer these, we use the language of counterfactuals to give two formalizations of "linear representation", one in the output (word) representation space, and one in the input (sentence) space. We then prove these connect to linear probing and model steering, respectively. To make sense of geometric notions, we use the formalization to identify a particular (non-Euclidean) inner product that respects language structure in a sense we make precise. Using this causal inner product, we show how to unify all notions of linear representation. In particular, this allows the construction of probes and steering vectors using counterfactual pairs. Experiments with LLaMA-2 demonstrate the existence of linear representations of concepts, the connection to interpretation and control, and the fundamental role of the choice of inner product.

papers.title: Testing Pre-trained Language Models’ Understanding of Distributivity via Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: To what extent do pre-trained language models grasp semantic knowledge regarding the phenomenon of distributivity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DistNLI, a diagnostic dataset for distributivity, and uses causal mediation analysis to show that pre-trained language models have some understanding of distributivity, which is associated with model size and vocabulary size, and that this knowledge is concentrated in middle layers.
papers.conclusion: Pre-trained language models have some understanding of distributivity, and causal mediation analysis reveals patterns in how this knowledge is encoded, particularly in middle layers.
papers.key_findings:
Models with more parameters tend to show understanding of distributivity, as measured by Total Effect (TE).
Models with richer vocabulary (larger vocabulary size) tend to show higher TE.
Knowledge of distributivity is concentrated in middle layers of the models.
The concentration of knowledge (as measured by Natural Indirect Effect) patterns with the magnitude of TE: models with higher TE have more concentrated NIEs.
papers.limitation:
The DistNLI dataset is limited to the phenomenon of distributivity of verb predication and should only be used as a diagnostic dataset for this specific phenomenon.
The dataset size is relatively small.
Some minimal pairs in the dataset might contradict world knowledge, though grammaticality is maintained.
future_direction: Increasing the diversity of predicates and subjects in DistNLI, e.g., to include more complicated combinations.
Investigating how robust the causal mediation analysis framework is to the definition of metrics, such as an empirical comparison between alternative definitions.
papers.abstract: To what extent do pre-trained language models grasp semantic knowledge regarding the phenomenon of distributivity? In this paper, we introduce DistNLI, a new diagnostic dataset for natural language inference that targets the semantic difference arising from distributivity, and employ the causal mediation analysis framework to quantify the model behavior and explore the underlying mechanism in this semantically-related task. We find that the extent of models’ understanding is associated with model size and vocabulary size. We also provide insights into how models encode such high-level semantic knowledge.

papers.title: Look Within, Why LLMs Hallucinate: A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: Do different self-attention layers of an LLM equally affect hallucinations? Can we alleviate the hallucinations through intervening self-attention layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to disable self-attention layers in LLMs to study their causal effect on hallucination, finding that disabling specific front or tail layers can alleviate hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The front or tail layers are most prone to convey hallucinations, and the middle layers may contain factual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Different self-attention layers affect hallucinations differently.
Front or tail layers are most prone to convey hallucinations.
Middle layers may contain factual knowledge, as disabling them degrades performance.
Disabling certain front or tail layers can alleviate hallucinations, as shown by increased accuracy on benchmarks.
The answers generated by LLMs change when specific attention layers are disabled.
papers.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) is a milestone in generative artificial intelligence, achieving significant success in text comprehension and generation tasks. Despite the tremendous success of LLMs in many downstream tasks, they suffer from severe hallucination problems, posing significant challenges to the practical applications of LLMs. Most of the works about LLMs' hallucinations focus on data quality. Self-attention is a core module in transformer-based LLMs, while its potential relationship with LLMs' hallucination has been hardly investigated. To fill this gap, we study this problem from a causal perspective. We propose a method to intervene in LLMs' self-attention layers and maintain their structures and sizes intact. Specifically, we disable different self-attention layers in several popular open-source LLMs and then compare their degrees of hallucination with the original ones. We evaluate the intervened LLMs on hallucination assessment benchmarks and conclude that disabling some specific self-attention layers in the front or tail of the LLMs can alleviate hallucination issues. The study paves a new way for understanding and mitigating LLMs' hallucinations.

papers.title: Faithful-Patchscopes: Understanding and Mitigating Model Bias in Hidden Representations Explanation of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how model bias induced by imbalanced linguistic patterns affects the faithfulness of hidden representation explanations in LLMs using Patchscopes, and proposes a method to mitigate this bias.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that model bias induced by imbalanced linguistic patterns undermines the faithfulness of hidden representation explanations in Patchscopes, and introduces BALOR, a contrastive logit-recalibration method that suppresses bias and amplifies contextual information during generation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that imbalanced linguistic patterns induce model bias that reduces Patchscopes' faithfulness, and BALOR effectively mitigates this bias through logit recalibration, improving explanation reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Model bias from imbalanced linguistic patterns causes an average 18.84% decrease in faithfulness of Patchscopes.
BALOR consistently outperforms existing baselines, achieving up to 33% relative improvement in explanation faithfulness.
Bias-sensitive layers can be located using logit difference and gradient similarity alignment metrics.
BALOR is robust across hyperparameters and decoding temperatures, with Shared mode being more stable than Divided mode.
The method improves faithfulness across multiple LLMs and tasks including color, gender, culture, and age.
papers.limitation: BALOR's Divided mode is less stable than Shared mode due to divergence between prompt sequences.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities for hidden representation interpretation through Patchscopes, a framework that uses LLMs themselves to generate human-readable explanations by decoding from internal hidden representations. However, our work shows that LLMs tend to rely on inherent linguistic patterns, which can override contextual information encoded in the hidden representations during decoding. For example, even when a hidden representation encodes the contextual attribute "purple" for "broccoli", LLMs still generate "green" in their explanations, reflecting a strong prior association. This behavior reveals a systematic unfaithfulness in Patchscopes. To systematically study this issue, we first designed a dataset to evaluate the faithfulness of Patchscopes under biased cases, and our results show that there is an 18.84\% faithfulness decrease on average. We then propose Bias Alignment through Logit Recalibration (BALOR), which treats the output logits from an unpatched prompt as capturing model bias and contrasts them with logits obtained under patched contextual information. By recalibrating the logit distribution through this contrast, BALOR suppresses model bias and amplifies contextual information during generation. Experiments across multiple LLMs demonstrate that BALOR consistently outperforms existing baselines, achieving up to 33\% relative performance improvement.

papers.title: Learning to Deceive with Attention-Based Explanations
papers.research_question: Do attention scores necessarily indicate features that influence a model's predictions? Can attention be manipulated to produce deceptive explanations while the model still relies on impermissible tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention mechanisms can be easily manipulated during training to produce deceptive explanations that assign low weight to impermissible tokens, while models continue to rely on those tokens for prediction, casting doubt on attention's reliability for auditing models.
papers.conclusion: Attention is easily manipulable with minimal accuracy cost, raising concerns about its use as a tool for model auditing and transparency.
papers.key_findings:
A simple training scheme can severely reduce attention mass on impermissible tokens with little to no decrease in task accuracy.
Human studies show that manipulated attention explanations deceive participants into thinking biased models do not rely on gender information.
Manipulated models cheat by passing information through recurrent connections or by increasing the magnitude of representations for impermissible tokens.
For sequence-to-sequence tasks, manipulated attention models outperform no-attention and uniform attention baselines, indicating attention adds value beyond alignment.
Different random seeds lead to different alternative mechanisms for maintaining performance while reducing attention on impermissible tokens.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms are ubiquitous components in neural architectures applied to natural language processing. In addition to yielding gains in predictive accuracy, attention weights are often claimed to confer interpretability, purportedly useful both for providing insights to practitioners and for explaining why a model makes its decisions to stakeholders. We call the latter use of attention mechanisms into question by demonstrating a simple method for training models to produce deceptive attention masks. Our method diminishes the total weight assigned to designated impermissible tokens, even when the models can be shown to nevertheless rely on these features to drive predictions. Across multiple models and tasks, our approach manipulates attention weights while paying surprisingly little cost in accuracy. Through a human study, we show that our manipulated attention-based explanations deceive people into thinking that predictions from a model biased against gender minorities do not rely on the gender. Consequently, our results cast doubt on attention's reliability as a tool for auditing algorithms in the context of fairness and accountability. 1

papers.title: Attributing Fair Decisions with Attention Interventions
papers.research_question: How can attention weights be used to attribute fairness and accuracy of a model, and how can bias be mitigated by manipulating attention weights?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an attention-based attribution framework that can identify features responsible for model fairness and accuracy, and proposes a post-processing bias mitigation strategy by manipulating attention weights.
papers.conclusion: The attention-based attribution framework is effective for fairness attribution and bias mitigation, providing interpretability and flexibility across tabular and text data.
papers.key_findings:
The attribution framework correctly identifies features responsible for accuracy and fairness in synthetic data.
The framework captures indirect discrimination where proxy features contribute more to unfairness than the sensitive attribute.
The post-processing mitigation strategy by reducing attention weights of unfair features is competitive with state-of-the-art methods.
The method is effective on both tabular and text data, reducing bias in occupation classification.
The method provides interpretability by showing which features are used for predictions.
papers.limitation:
The framework may be used for fairwashing (generating fake explanations for unfair decisions).
The framework is vulnerable to adversarial attacks.
The method does not achieve the best accuracy-fairness trade-off on the UCI Adult dataset for statistical parity.
future_direction: Improving the fairness-accuracy trade-off by considering the trade-off each feature contributes to both accuracy and fairness.
papers.abstract: The widespread use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in consequential domains, such as healthcare and parole decision-making systems, has drawn intense scrutiny on the fairness of these methods. However, ensuring fairness is often insufficient as the rationale for a contentious decision needs to be audited, understood, and defended. We propose that the attention mechanism can be used to ensure fair outcomes while simultaneously providing feature attributions to account for how a decision was made. Toward this goal, we design an attention-based model that can be leveraged as an attribution framework. It can identify features responsible for both performance and fairness of the model through attention interventions and attention weight manipulation. Using this attribution framework, we then design a post-processing bias mitigation strategy and compare it with a suite of baselines. We demonstrate the versatility of our approach by conducting experiments on two distinct data types, tabular and textual.

papers.title: Semantic and Structural Analysis of Implicit Biases in Large Language Models: An Interpretable Approach
papers.research_question: How to identify and explain implicit stereotypes in large language models using an interpretable bias detection method?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an interpretable bias detection method for large language models that integrates nested semantic representation with attention perturbation to identify hidden social biases in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The interpretable detection method effectively identifies implicit biases in LLMs, improving detection accuracy and semantic consistency, and provides a foundation for bias intervention and ethical deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves higher bias detection accuracy (84.7%), semantic consistency (91.2%), and lower contextual sensitivity (8.5) compared to baselines.
It demonstrates strong generalization across multiple stereotype dimensions, with higher accuracy for gender and profession than for religion and race.
Higher semantic similarity between texts leads to more consistent bias judgments, reducing conflict rates.
Attention perturbation analysis reveals the model's sensitivity to social attribute terms, helping uncover bias pathways.
The method provides interpretable insights into how implicit stereotypes are formed in language models.
papers.limitation: Performance declines on more complex, culturally embedded biases such as religion and race due to their subtlety and ambiguity.
future_direction: Expand the method's adaptability to cross-cultural and multilingual contexts.
Integrate external knowledge bases and user feedback signals for more flexible bias detection.
Embed interpretability mechanisms into model interaction interfaces for user perception and response.
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the issue of implicit stereotypes that may arise during the generation process of large language models. It proposes an interpretable bias detection method aimed at identifying hidden social biases in model outputs, especially those semantic tendencies that are not easily captured through explicit linguistic features. The method combines nested semantic representation with a contextual contrast mechanism. It extracts latent bias features from the vector space structure of model outputs. Using attention weight perturbation, it analyzes the model's sensitivity to specific social attribute terms, thereby revealing the semantic pathways through which bias is formed. To validate the effectiveness of the method, this study uses the StereoSet dataset, which covers multiple stereotype dimensions including gender, profession, religion, and race. The evaluation focuses on several key metrics, such as bias detection accuracy, semantic consistency, and contextual sensitivity. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves strong detection performance across various dimensions. It can accurately identify bias differences between semantically similar texts while maintaining high semantic alignment and output stability. The method also demonstrates high interpretability in its structural design. It helps uncover the internal bias association mechanisms within language models. This provides a more transparent and reliable technical foundation for bias detection. The approach is suitable for real-world applications where high trustworthiness of generated content is required.

papers.title: Unveiling the "Fairness Seesaw": Discovering and Mitigating Gender and Race Bias in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) yield gender and race bias in responses? Do VLMs have reliable confidence levels in different social groups? How can we mitigate these biases?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers the 'Fairness Seesaw' phenomenon in Vision-Language Models and proposes RES-FAIR, a post-hoc method that mitigates gender and race bias by projecting hidden states away from biased residual directions and amplifying fair components.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a new lens for understanding how multi-modal models store and process sensitive social information and demonstrates an effective post-hoc method for bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
The Fairness Paradox: Models often generate 'fair' text labels while maintaining highly skewed confidence scores toward specific social groups.
Layer-wise Fluctuation: Fairness knowledge peaks in intermediate layers and undergoes substantial 'knowledge erosion' in the final layers.
Residual Discrepancy: Within a single hidden layer, different residual streams carry conflicting social knowledge—some reinforcing fairness while others amplifying bias.
RES-FAIR significantly improves response fairness and confidence calibration without compromising general reasoning abilities.
State-of-the-art VLMs still struggle to produce fair responses and have mis-calibrated confidence distributions.
papers.limitation: The study of race is limited to 'black' and 'white' categories due to dataset constraints, which is expandable in future work.
future_direction: Expanding the study to include more race labels beyond 'black' and 'white'.
papers.abstract: Although Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable success, the knowledge mechanisms underlying their social biases remain a black box, where fairness- and ethics-related problems harm certain groups of people in society. It is unknown to what extent VLMs yield gender and race bias in generative responses. In this paper, we conduct a systematic discovery of gender and race bias in state-of-the-art VLMs, focusing not only on surface-level responses but also on the internal probability distributions and hidden state dynamics. Our empirical analysis reveals three critical findings: 1) The Fairness Paradox: Models often generate fair text labels while maintaining highly skewed confidence scores (mis-calibration) toward specific social groups. 2) Layer-wise Fluctuation: Fairness knowledge is not uniformly distributed; it peaks in intermediate layers and undergoes substantial knowledge erosion in the final layers. 3) Residual Discrepancy: Within a single hidden layer, different residual streams carry conflicting social knowledge - some reinforcing fairness while others amplifying bias. Leveraging these insights, we propose RES-FAIR (RESidual Flow Adjustment for Inference Recalibration), a post-hoc framework that mitigates bias by localizing and projecting hidden states away from biased residual directions while amplifying fair components. Evaluations on PAIRS and SocialCounterfactuals datasets demonstrate that our discovery-based approach significantly improves response fairness and confidence calibration without compromising general reasoning abilities. Our work provides a new lens for understanding how multi-modal models store and process sensitive social information.

papers.title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
papers.research_question: How can we enhance multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) in LLMs simultaneously without training, by controlling sparse activations in specific model components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that enhances multiple trustworthiness dimensions in LLMs by identifying sparse, task-specific attention heads and controlling their representations using Gaussian Mixture Models, avoiding control conflicts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Activation Control is an effective training-free method for enhancing multi-dimensional trustworthiness in LLMs by leveraging sparse and independent task-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Activation Control can enhance safety, factuality, and bias simultaneously without significant interference, outperforming representation engineering baselines in multi-task control.
Attention heads for different tasks are sparse and have minimal overlap, allowing independent control.
The method does not significantly harm general model performance on MMLU and CSQA.
The method generalizes to other models (Qwen series) and additional trustworthiness tasks (robustness, privacy).
Control shifts head outputs towards task-relevant tokens, as shown by unembedding projections.
papers.limitation:
Relies on construction of paired stimuli, which may require domain knowledge.
Experiments are limited to a few models and tasks.
future_direction: Extend to more tasks and models
Explore theoretical foundations of sparsity
papers.abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality. In this work, we address this issue through ``Sparse Activation Control''. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint components that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e., attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factuality, and bias concurrently.

papers.title: Interpreting Gender Bias in Neural Machine Translation: Multilingual Architecture Matters
papers.research_question: Does the multilingual neural machine translation architecture impact the degree of gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language-specific encoder-decoders exhibit less gender bias than shared architectures, and proposes two interpretability methods based on source embeddings and attention to explain this difference.
papers.conclusion: The choice of multilingual architecture impacts gender bias in machine translation, and the proposed interpretability methods help explain why language-specific models perform better by showing they encode more gender information and have more diverted attention.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific encoder-decoders show less gender bias than shared encoder-decoders when trained on the same data.
Language-specific models encode more gender information in source embeddings, as measured by SVM classification accuracy.
Language-specific models have more diverted attention, allowing them to consider a broader context when predicting gender.
Bilingual systems vary in the amount of gender information encoded in embeddings depending on the target language.
Most gender translation errors involve assuming masculine occupations, which may be due to data imbalances and linguistic/cultural factors.
papers.limitation: The conclusions are based on the WinoMT benchmark, which has known downsides such as unnaturalness and logical failures, potentially affecting the results.
future_direction: Providing real-world data benchmarks to evaluate gender accuracy in machine translation systems.
Experimenting with more distant language pairs to see if the conclusions hold.
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation architectures mainly differ in the number of sharing modules and parameters applied among languages. In this paper, and from an algorithmic perspective, we explore whether the chosen architecture, when trained with the same data, influences the level of gender bias. Experiments conducted in three language pairs show that language-specific encoder-decoders exhibit less bias than the shared architecture. We propose two methods for interpreting and studying gender bias in machine translation based on source embeddings and attention. Our analysis shows that, in the language-specific case, the embeddings encode more gender information, and their attention is more diverted. Both behaviors help in mitigating gender bias.

papers.title: DICE: Detecting In-distribution Contamination in LLM's Fine-tuning Phase for Math Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does in-distribution contamination contribute to a model’s overall math reasoning ability, and if not, how can we detect it to prevent overestimating the model’s capabilities due to contamination?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DICE, a locate-then-detect method that uses internal states of LLMs to detect in-distribution contamination with high accuracy and generalization.
papers.conclusion: DICE effectively detects in-distribution contamination by leveraging internal states, outperforming existing methods and generalizing across datasets and models.
papers.key_findings:
In-distribution contamination inflates performance on in-distribution tasks but does not improve out-of-distribution performance, indicating it does not enhance general reasoning ability.
DICE achieves near 100% AUROC in detecting in-distribution contamination, significantly outperforming baseline methods like perplexity and Min-k Prob.
The most sensitive layer to contamination (contamination layer) can be located by maximum Euclidean distance in hidden states, and using this layer's features yields the best detection performance.
DICE generalizes well to unseen in-distribution datasets and can distinguish between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data.
DICE's contamination predictions correlate with LLM performance on benchmarks (R² between 0.61 and 0.75), providing a way to estimate performance without decoding.
papers.limitation: DICE is only evaluated on math reasoning tasks and LLMs, and its applicability to other NLP tasks and model types remains to be explored.
future_direction: Extend DICE to detect contamination in other NLP tasks like text classification and summarization.
Explore DICE in other types of LLMs or even vision models.
papers.abstract: The advancement of large language models (LLMs) relies on evaluation using public benchmarks, but data contamination can lead to overestimated performance. Previous researches focus on detecting contamination by determining whether the model has seen the exact same data during training. Besides, prior work has already shown that even training on data similar to benchmark data inflates performance, namely \emph{In-distribution contamination}. In this work, we argue that in-distribution contamination can lead to the performance drop on OOD benchmarks. To effectively detect in-distribution contamination, we propose DICE, a novel method that leverages the internal states of LLMs to locate-then-detect the contamination. DICE first identifies the most sensitive layer to contamination, then trains a classifier based on the internal states of that layer. Experiments reveal DICE's high accuracy in detecting in-distribution contamination across various LLMs and math reasoning datasets. We also show the generalization capability of the trained DICE detector, which is able to detect contamination across multiple benchmarks with similar distributions. Additionally, we find that DICE's predictions correlate with the performance of LLMs fine-tuned by either us or other organizations, achieving a coefficient of determination ($R^2$) between 0.61 and 0.75. The code and data are available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/DICE.

papers.title: Addressing divergent representations from causal interventions on neural networks
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether causal interventions on neural networks create out-of-distribution (divergent) representations and whether this affects the faithfulness of the resulting explanations to the target model in its natural state.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that causal interventions often produce representations that diverge from the model's natural distribution, analyzes when such divergence is harmless or pernicious, and introduces a modified CL loss to mitigate pernicious divergence.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that divergent representations are a common issue in causal interventions, but by understanding and mitigating them (e.g., with the CL loss), we can move towards more reliable interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
Causal interventions (e.g., activation patching, DAS) often produce representations that diverge from the model's natural distribution.
