A particularly challenging variant, knowledge overshadowing, occurs when one piece of activated knowledge inadvertently masks another relevant piece, leading to erroneous outputs even with high-quality training data. Current understanding of overshadowing is largely confined to inference-time observations, lacking deep insights into its origins and internal mechanisms during model training. Therefore, we introduce PhantomCircuit, a novel framework designed to comprehensively analyze and detect knowledge overshadowing. By innovatively employing knowledge circuit analysis, PhantomCircuit dissects the function of key components in the circuit and how the attention pattern dynamics contribute to the overshadowing phenomenon and its evolution throughout the training process. Extensive experiments demonstrate PhantomCircuit's effectiveness in identifying such instances, offering novel insights into this elusive hallucination and providing the research community with a new methodological lens for its potential mitigation.

papers.title: On the Universal Truthfulness Hyperplane Inside LLMs
papers.research_question: Does a universal truthfulness hyperplane exist within LLMs that can distinguish factually correct and incorrect outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing the diversity of training datasets significantly enhances the generalization of truthfulness probes, supporting the hypothesis that a universal truthfulness hyperplane exists within LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The findings support the existence of a universal truthfulness hyperplane in LLMs, offering directions for future research on hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on diverse datasets achieve ~70% cross-task accuracy, outperforming baselines like Self-Eval and Probability.
Attention head outputs are more effective for probing truthfulness than layer residual activations.
Increasing dataset diversity improves generalization more than increasing sample size.
The universal truthfulness hyperplane is more pronounced in advanced models like Mistral-7b and LLaMA2-13b-chat.
Probes trained on single datasets like TruthfulQA fail to generalize out-of-distribution, indicating overfitting.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various fields, hallucination remains a significant challenge. Recent studies have explored hallucinations through the lens of internal representations, proposing mechanisms to decipher LLMs' adherence to facts. However, these approaches often fail to generalize to out-of-distribution data, leading to concerns about whether internal representation patterns reflect fundamental factual awareness, or only overfit spurious correlations on the specific datasets. In this work, we investigate whether a universal truthfulness hyperplane that distinguishes the model's factually correct and incorrect outputs exists within the model. To this end, we scale up the number of training datasets and conduct an extensive evaluation -- we train the truthfulness hyperplane on a diverse collection of over 40 datasets and examine its cross-task, cross-domain, and in-domain generalization. Our results indicate that increasing the diversity of the training datasets significantly enhances the performance in all scenarios, while the volume of data samples plays a less critical role. This finding supports the optimistic hypothesis that a universal truthfulness hyperplane may indeed exist within the model, offering promising directions for future research.

papers.title: LLM Assertiveness can be Mechanistically Decomposed into Emotional and Logical Components
papers.research_question: What is the internal basis of LLM assertiveness, and can it be decomposed into separable components like emotional and logical persuasion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM assertiveness can be mechanistically decomposed into orthogonal emotional and logical components, providing evidence for a multi-component structure similar to human persuasion models.
papers.conclusion: The study provides mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlights avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers (5-6) are most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts.
High-assertive representations decompose into orthogonal emotional and logical clusters.
Emotional steering vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, whereas logical vectors have more localized effects.
papers.limitation:
The model is small (1B parameters), so scaling effects are uncertain.
Only one architecture is examined, limiting cross-model generality.
Dataset size is modest (n=645), which may obscure finer-grained cues.
Cluster interpretation relies on manual inspection.
future_direction: Develop more automated approaches for cluster interpretation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often display overconfidence, presenting information with unwarranted certainty in high-stakes contexts. We investigate the internal basis of this behavior via mechanistic interpretability. Using open-sourced Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on human annotated assertiveness datasets, we extract residual activations across all layers, and compute similarity metrics to localize assertive representations. Our analysis identifies layers most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts and reveals that high-assertive representations decompose into two orthogonal sub-components of emotional and logical clusters-paralleling the dual-route Elaboration Likelihood Model in Psychology. Steering vectors derived from these sub-components show distinct causal effects: emotional vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, while logical vectors exert more localized effects. These findings provide mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlight avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.

papers.title: SAE-SSV: Supervised Steering in Sparse Representation Spaces for Reliable Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reliably control large language model behavior in open-ended generation settings by using supervised steering in sparse, interpretable representation spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a supervised steering framework (SAE-SSV) that constrains interventions to a sparse, task-relevant latent subspace identified via labeled data and sparse autoencoders, enabling more targeted control and better preservation of generation quality.
papers.conclusion: SAE-SSV enables effective LLM steering by operating in sparse, task-specific subspaces, outperforming existing methods and providing a more targeted and interpretable approach to behavior control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-SSV consistently outperforms baseline steering methods (CAA, RePe, Top PC, ITI) in steering success rate across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity tasks.
A notably small subspace of SAE latent dimensions is sufficient for effective steering, enabling targeted and interpretable interventions.
Steering in the structured SAE subspace preserves or improves generation quality (lexical diversity, entropy) compared to baselines, which often degrade it.
The method generalizes to unseen datasets within the same task domain, capturing both semantic directions and stylistic patterns.
The top SAE features used for steering are interpretable and correspond to semantically meaningful concepts related to the target attribute.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to pretrained sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which may not be available for all models or domains.
Only evaluated on LLMs with up to 9B parameters; scaling to larger models is future work.
Evaluation focused on open-ended generation tasks with limited human evaluation; generalizability to more specialized domains remains to be explored.
future_direction: Achieve universal and style-invariant SSVs that generalize across datasets, tasks, and model families by curating diverse training corpora and developing objectives that encourage semantic steering while minimizing stylistic sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in natural language understanding and generation, but controlling their behavior reliably remains challenging, especially in open-ended generation settings. This paper introduces a novel supervised steering approach that operates in sparse, interpretable representation spaces. We employ sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to obtain sparse latent representations that aim to disentangle semantic attributes from model activations. Then we train linear classifiers to identify a small subspace of task-relevant dimensions in latent representations. Finally, we learn supervised steering vectors constrained to this subspace, optimized to align with target behaviors. Experiments across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity steering tasks with multiple LLMs demonstrate that our supervised steering vectors achieve higher success rates with minimal degradation in generation quality compared to existing methods. Further analysis reveals that a notably small subspace is sufficient for effective steering, enabling more targeted and interpretable interventions. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Ineedanamehere/SAE-SSV.

papers.title: Beyond Prompt Engineering: Robust Behavior Control in LLMs via Steering Target Atoms
papers.research_question: How can we achieve precise control over language model generation by isolating and manipulating disentangled knowledge components (target atoms) using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Steering Target Atoms (STA), a method that uses sparse autoencoders to identify and manipulate disentangled knowledge components (target atoms) for precise behavior control in LLMs, demonstrating improved safety control and robustness compared to prompt engineering.
papers.conclusion: STA provides a novel method for precise behavior control in LLMs, effective in safety and reasoning domains, and steering techniques offer robustness and flexibility advantages over prompt engineering.
papers.key_findings:
STA achieves better detoxification performance than baselines, increasing average detoxification from 59.97% to 83.45% in Gemma-2-9B-pt.
Steering techniques exhibit superior robustness and flexibility compared to prompt-based approaches, especially in adversarial scenarios.
Steering can effectively control reasoning length in large reasoning models, mitigating overthinking.
Steering vectors remain powerful even with few instances (e.g., 4 samples).
Steering in intermediate layers (layers 24-25) is more effective for behavior control.
papers.limitation:
SAE-based methods may underperform simple baselines in some steering tasks, and STA shows limited effectiveness in the personality domain.
Experiments are limited to Gemma and Llama models due to limited publicly accessible SAEs.
The applicability to other nuanced domains like multi-turn dialogue or complex reasoning tasks remains to be validated.
future_direction: Extend STA to a broader range of LLMs, including larger and more diverse architectures.
Investigate the underlying causes of performance divergence in the personality domain.
Explore comparison with many-shot prompting for jailbreaking.
papers.abstract: Mengru Wang, Ziwen Xu, Shengyu Mao, Shumin Deng, Zhaopeng Tu, Huajun Chen, Ningyu Zhang. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: A large-scale examination of inductive biases shaping high-level visual representation in brains and machines
papers.research_question: How do different inductive biases (architecture, task objective, visual training diet) affect the emergent brain alignment of learned visual representations in artificial neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Visual training diet (dataset diversity) has the largest effect on brain predictivity, while architecture and task objective have smaller effects when controlled; many models achieve similarly high brain predictivity despite different representations, suggesting standard linking methods may be too flexible.
papers.conclusion: Dataset diversity is a key factor in developing brain-aligned visual representations, and current model-to-brain linking methods may need to be refined to better capture representational differences.
papers.key_findings:
CNN and transformer architectures achieve near equivalent brain predictivity when trained on the same dataset and task.
Instance-level contrastive learning objectives lead to more brain-predictive representations than non-contrastive self-supervised objectives.
Vision-language alignment (e.g., CLIP) does not consistently yield higher brain predictivity compared to purely visual contrastive learning when controlling for dataset.
Visual training diet (dataset diversity) has the largest effect on brain predictivity, with models trained on more diverse datasets (e.g., OpenAI's 400M dataset) performing best.
Many models achieve similarly high brain predictivity after feature re-weighting, suggesting that standard linking methods may be too flexible to capture representational differences.
papers.limitation: The two linking methods (classical RSA and voxel-encoding RSA) give different estimates of explained variance, and it is unclear which is more correct.
future_direction: Developing better metrics for dataset diversity and richness.
Refining model-to-brain linking methods to be less flexible and more diagnostic.
Exploring one-to-one mappings between model units and brain neurons, and expanding brain targets to include topographic organization.
papers.abstract: The rapid release of high-performing computer vision models offers new potential to study the impact of different inductive biases on the emergent brain alignment of learned representations. Here, we perform controlled comparisons among a curated set of 224 diverse models to test the impact of specific model properties on visual brain predictivity - a process requiring over 1.8 billion regressions and 50.3 thousand representational similarity analyses. We find that models with qualitatively different architectures (e.g. CNNs versus Transformers) and task objectives (e.g. purely visual contrastive learning versus vision- language alignment) achieve near equivalent brain predictivity, when other factors are held constant. Instead, variation across visual training diets yields the largest, most consistent effect on brain predictivity. Many models achieve similarly high brain predictivity, despite clear variation in their underlying representations - suggesting that standard methods used to link models to brains may be too flexible. Broadly, these findings challenge common assumptions about the factors underlying emergent brain alignment, and outline how we can leverage controlled model comparison to probe the common computational principles underlying biological and artificial visual systems.

papers.title: System-Mediated Attention Imbalances Make Vision-Language Models Say Yes
papers.research_question: Does system-mediated attention imbalance (redundant system attention leading to insufficient image and text attention) cause the yes-bias hallucination in vision-language models, as opposed to the image-centric hypothesis?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that system-mediated attention imbalances (redundant system attention causing insufficient image and text attention) are a key factor in the yes-bias hallucination in VLMs, and that redistributing attention from the system modality to image and text modalities effectively suppresses this bias.
papers.conclusion: System-mediated attention imbalances are a key driver of the yes-bias in VLMs, and redistributing system attention to image and text modalities is an effective mitigation strategy, highlighting the importance of a holistic view of attention allocation.
papers.key_findings:
Redistributing system attention to image and text modalities substantially suppresses the yes-bias, outperforming image-centric and text-suppressing methods.
The yes-bias is driven by redundant system attention in late decoder layers, which causes attention imbalances harming both image and text processing.
System-mediated attention imbalances encourage reliance on coarse input representations, which is detrimental for compositional tasks requiring fine-grained analysis.
The system-mediated hypothesis is empirically superior to the image-centric hypothesis for the yes-bias.
The effects of attention redistribution vary across tasks and model scales, with larger models showing less consistent gains.
papers.limitation:
Focus on LLaVA-based architectures and single-token generation in yes/no contexts, limiting generality.
Use of zero-ablation with complete redistribution prevents exploration of partial redistributions.
Interventions at the quarter level due to computational constraints, precluding per-layer analysis.
Representation-level mechanisms are inferred from performance and attention weights, not directly probed.
future_direction: Explore implications for autoregressive hallucination.
Apply holistic causal interventions to other manifestations of VLM hallucination.
Investigate redundant system attention in text-only LLMs.
papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) hallucination is commonly linked to imbalanced allocation of attention across input modalities: system, image and text. However, existing mitigation strategies tend towards an image-centric interpretation of these imbalances, often prioritising increased image attention while giving less consideration to the roles of the other modalities. In this study, we evaluate a more holistic, system-mediated account, which attributes these imbalances to functionally redundant system weights that reduce attention to image and textual inputs. We show that this framework offers a useful empirical perspective on the yes-bias, a common form of hallucination in which VLMs indiscriminately respond 'yes'. Causally redistributing attention from the system modality to image and textual inputs substantially suppresses this bias, often outperforming existing approaches. We further present evidence suggesting that system-mediated attention imbalances contribute to the yes-bias by encouraging a default reliance on coarse input representations, which are effective for some tasks but ill-suited to others. Taken together, these findings firmly establish system attention as a key factor in VLM hallucination and highlight its potential as a lever for mitigation.

papers.title: Dissecting Lottery Ticket Transformers: Structural and Behavioral Study\n of Sparse Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does iterative magnitude pruning affect the learned representations and internal components of Transformers for neural machine translation, and what are the differences in behavior between sparse and dense models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that iterative magnitude pruning degrades complex semantic knowledge first, causes higher layers to diverge and become less complex, shifts encoding burden to early layers, and leaves attention mechanisms largely unchanged.
papers.conclusion: The paper evaluates how unstructured pruning affects Transformer behavior while task performance is maintained, showing pruning degrades semantic knowledge before BLEU, early sparse layers better encode low-level information, representational changes occur especially in higher layers, and attention distributions remain similar.
papers.key_findings:
Complex semantic information is lost first during pruning, before BLEU decreases.
Model activations steadily diverge from unpruned representations, particularly at higher layers.
Information flow becomes more distributed in sparse Transformers: lower layers perform more encoding.
Attention mechanisms remain remarkably consistent across sparsities.
Encoder-decoder attention is the richest in representation, whereas decoder self-attention is the simplest.
papers.limitation:
BLEU is an imperfect measure of translation quality, so pruned models might perform worse than suggested.
The work focuses solely on magnitude pruning, which may not be representative of other pruning methods.
Probing classifiers measure correlation between model outputs and auxiliary information, not necessarily what information the model uses during its forward pass.
future_direction: Future work could analyze a model's encoded knowledge in other ways beyond probing.
Differences in how directly sparse and dense models encode information could be studied using minimum description lengths.
papers.abstract:
Recent work on the lottery ticket hypothesis has produced highly sparse
Transformers for NMT while maintaining BLEU. However, it is unclear how such
pruning techniques affect a model's learned representations. By probing
Transformers with more and more low-magnitude weights pruned away, we find that
complex semantic information is first to be degraded. Analysis of internal
activations reveals that higher layers diverge most over the course of pruning,
gradually becoming less complex than their dense counterparts. Meanwhile, early
layers of sparse models begin to perform more encoding. Attention mechanisms
remain remarkably consistent as sparsity increases.

papers.title: Personality Alignment of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can large language models be aligned with the unique personality traits and preferences of individual users, as opposed to general human values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel personality alignment framework comprising the PAPI dataset for evaluating alignment across positive and negative personality dimensions and the PAS method, which efficiently aligns LLMs to individual preferences via activation interventions without weight updates.
papers.conclusion: Personality alignment is a crucial step towards human-centered AI, and the proposed PAS method provides an efficient, training-free approach to tailor LLM behavior to individual user preferences, paving the way for more meaningful AI interactions.
papers.key_findings:
The PAS method achieves superior personality alignment performance compared to DPO and PPO, requiring only 1/5 of the optimization time.
PAS applied to Llama-3-8B-Instruct can outperform the GPT-4o model on personality alignment tasks.
The PAPI dataset, with over 320,000 samples from multiple personality inventories, enables comprehensive evaluation of LLM alignment across both adaptive and maladaptive personality traits.
Activation interventions for personality alignment are highly parameter-efficient, storing only about 1/10,000,000 of the parameters compared to a full-parameter model.
The method demonstrates generalization capabilities in open-ended generation and complex reasoning tasks while maintaining aligned personality traits.
papers.abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) typically aim to reflect general human values and behaviors, but they often fail to capture the unique characteristics and preferences of individual users. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of Personality Alignment. This approach tailors LLMs' responses and decisions to match the specific preferences of individual users or closely related groups. Inspired by psychometrics, we created the Personality Alignment with Personality Inventories (PAPI) dataset, which includes data from over 320,000 real subjects across multiple personality assessments, including both the Big Five Personality Factors and Dark Triad traits. This comprehensive dataset enables quantitative evaluation of LLMs' alignment capabilities across both positive and potentially problematic personality dimensions. Recognizing the challenges of personality alignments, such as limited personal data, diverse preferences, and scalability requirements, we developed an activation intervention optimization method. This method enhances LLMs' ability to efficiently align with individual behavioral preferences using minimal data and computational resources. Remarkably, our method, PAS, achieves superior performance while requiring only 1/5 of the optimization time compared to DPO, offering practical value for personality alignment. Our work paves the way for future AI systems to make decisions and reason in truly personality ways, enhancing the relevance and meaning of AI interactions for each user and advancing human-centered artificial intelligence. The dataset and code are released at https://github.com/zhu-minjun/PAlign.

papers.title: AntiLeakBench: Preventing Data Contamination by Automatically Constructing Benchmarks with Updated Real-World Knowledge
papers.research_question: How to prevent data contamination in LLM evaluation by constructing benchmarks with updated real-world knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes AntiLeakBench, an automated anti-leakage benchmarking framework that constructs test samples with updated real-world knowledge to ensure strictly contamination-free evaluation of LLMs.
papers.conclusion: AntiLeakBench is an effective framework for contamination-free evaluation, providing accurate and fair assessments for LLMs with an automated building workflow.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-cutoff samples (with knowledge before the cutoff time) are likely contaminated and inflate LLM performance.
Post-cutoff samples (with knowledge after the cutoff time) are contamination-free and more accurately assess LLMs, as models must rely on context understanding rather than prior knowledge.
AntiLeakBench poses a significant challenge for LLMs, with most models scoring below 50 in EM and F1.
Proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4o) outperform open-source models by a large margin.
Multi-choice format is easier than generation format, and multi-hop tasks are more challenging than single-hop tasks.
papers.limitation:
The framework currently focuses on question-answering tasks; more diverse tasks could be explored in the future.
Relies on Wikidata and Wikipedia as data sources, which may have limitations.
future_direction: Explore more diverse tasks beyond question-answering for contamination-free evaluation.
Improve the data sources and methods for constructing high-quality samples automatically.
papers.abstract: Data contamination hinders fair LLM evaluation by introducing test data into newer models' training sets. Existing studies solve this challenge by updating benchmarks with newly collected data. However, they fail to guarantee contamination-free evaluation as the newly collected data may contain pre-existing knowledge, and their benchmark updates rely on intensive human labor. To address these issues, we in this paper propose AntiLeak-Bench, an automated anti-leakage benchmarking framework. Instead of simply using newly collected data, we construct samples with explicitly new knowledge absent from LLMs' training sets, which thus ensures strictly contamination-free evaluation. We further design a fully automated workflow to build and update our benchmark without human labor. This significantly reduces the cost of benchmark maintenance to accommodate emerging LLMs. Through extensive experiments, we highlight that data contamination likely exists before LLMs' cutoff time and demonstrate AntiLeak-Bench effectively overcomes this challenge.

papers.title: Causality is Key for Interpretability Claims to Generalise
papers.research_question: How can interpretability claims be made more rigorous and generalizable? The paper argues that causal inference specifies what constitutes a valid mapping from model activations to invariant high-level structures and the evidence needed to support such claims.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a causal framework for interpretability, arguing that claims should be stated in the language of causal inference and identifiability to ensure they generalize. It uses Pearl's causal hierarchy to diagnose claim-evidence mismatches and causal representation learning to specify assumptions.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability claims should be grounded in causal inference to ensure they generalize, and practitioners should use a causal framework to align methods, evidence, and claims.
papers.key_findings:
There is a frequent gap between the evidence provided by interpretability methods (e.g., associational) and the strength of the claims made (e.g., interventional or counterfactual).
A pilot study of 50 papers found roughly half of interpretability claims can admit a stronger interpretation than the evidence supports, indicating a field-wide terminological challenge.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research on large language models (LLMs) has yielded important insights into model behaviour, yet recurring pitfalls persist: findings that do not generalise, and causal interpretations that outrun the evidence. Our position is that causal inference specifies what constitutes a valid mapping from model activations to invariant high-level structures, the data or assumptions needed to achieve it, and the inferences it can support. Specifically, Pearl's causal hierarchy clarifies what an interpretability study can justify. Observations establish associations between model behaviour and internal components. Interventions (e.g., ablations or activation patching) support claims how these edits affect a behavioural metric (\eg, average change in token probabilities) over a set of prompts. However, counterfactual claims -- i.e., asking what the model output would have been for the same prompt under an unobserved intervention -- remain largely unverifiable without controlled supervision. We show how causal representation learning (CRL) operationalises this hierarchy, specifying which variables are recoverable from activations and under what assumptions. Together, these motivate a diagnostic framework that helps practitioners select methods and evaluations matching claims to evidence such that findings generalise.

papers.title: Beyond the Black Box: Interpretability of LLMs in Finance
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability techniques be applied to understand and control the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) in financial applications to improve transparency and reliability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates the application of mechanistic interpretability techniques—Logit Lens, Attribution Patching, and Sparse Autoencoders—to financial use cases, showing how they can be used to understand, debug, and steer model behavior for tasks like sentiment analysis, bias detection, and hallucination reduction.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability offers a promising path to dissect and guide AI-driven financial decisions with greater transparency and control, though challenges in scalability, generalization, and mapping abstract features to human-understandable concepts remain.
papers.key_findings:
Logit Lens analysis reveals how token prediction probabilities evolve across transformer layers in response to financial prompts, showing refinement of predictions in deeper layers.
Attribution Patching identifies specific attention heads in layers 8 and 10 of GPT-2 as causally significant for correct financial predictions.
Sparse Autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from model activations relevant to financial concepts like credit risk.
Feature steering via Sparse Autoencoders can modify model outputs, such as improving sentiment classification accuracy for credit risk analysis without fine-tuning.
A feature-activation-thresholded Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach can reduce hallucinations in financial question-answering by ensuring external factual data is incorporated when internal feature activations are low.
papers.limitation:
Scalability is a major concern, as manual circuit analysis becomes infeasible for very large models, and automated interpretability tools are still in early development.
Many techniques fail to generalize effectively to real-world financial applications, as models often rely on abstract representations not directly mappable to human-understandable financial concepts.
The evolving nature of financial markets and regulations means models trained on historical data may struggle to adapt, requiring dynamic interpretability pipelines.
Identifying a particular neuron or attention head does not always clarify the exact influence of features such as credit score or volatility on the final decision.
future_direction: Integrating mechanistic interpretability with feature-level attributions to ensure AI decisions are explainable in terms of real-world financial indicators.
Developing a hybrid approach that integrates traditional statistical modeling techniques using financial time series data with unstructured data processed by LLMs.
Building fully integrated interpretability tooling that combines techniques from various research efforts to streamline analysis workflows for financial professionals.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across a spectrum of tasks in financial services, including report generation, chatbots, sentiment analysis, regulatory compliance, investment advisory, financial knowledge retrieval, and summarization. However, their intrinsic complexity and lack of transparency pose significant challenges, especially in the highly regulated financial sector, where interpretability, fairness, and accountability are critical. As far as we are aware, this paper presents the first application in the finance domain of understanding and utilizing the inner workings of LLMs through mechanistic interpretability, addressing the pressing need for transparency and control in AI systems. Mechanistic interpretability is the most intuitive and transparent way to understand LLM behavior by reverse-engineering their internal workings. By dissecting the activations and circuits within these models, it provides insights into how specific features or components influence predictions - making it possible not only to observe but also to modify model behavior. In this paper, we explore the theoretical aspects of mechanistic interpretability and demonstrate its practical relevance through a range of financial use cases and experiments, including applications in trading strategies, sentiment analysis, bias, and hallucination detection. While not yet widely adopted, mechanistic interpretability is expected to become increasingly vital as adoption of LLMs increases. Advanced interpretability tools can ensure AI systems remain ethical, transparent, and aligned with evolving financial regulations. In this paper, we have put special emphasis on how these techniques can help unlock interpretability requirements for regulatory and compliance purposes - addressing both current needs and anticipating future expectations from financial regulators globally.

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models rely less consistently on the subspace mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies.
Findings are based on a specific reverse dictionary task and may not generalize to all reasoning contexts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit emergent behaviors suggestive of human-like reasoning. While recent work has identified structured, human-like conceptual representations within these models, it remains unclear whether they functionally rely on such representations for reasoning. Here we investigate the internal processing of LLMs during in-context concept inference. Our results reveal a conceptual subspace emerging in middle to late layers, whose representational structure persists across contexts. Using causal mediation analyses, we demonstrate that this subspace is not merely an epiphenomenon but is functionally central to model predictions, establishing its causal role in inference. We further identify a layer-wise progression where attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace, which is subsequently leveraged by later layers to generate predictions. Together, these findings provide evidence that LLMs dynamically construct and use structured, latent representations in context for inference, offering insights into the computational processes underlying flexible adaptation.

papers.title: Axiomatic Causal Interventions for Reverse Engineering Relevance Computation in Neural Retrieval Models
papers.research_question: How do neural retrieval models determine relevance, and can we isolate internal components that satisfy term-frequency axioms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends activation patching to neural retrieval models and uses it to localize attention heads that encode a term frequency signal aligned with the TFC1 axiom in TAS-B.
papers.conclusion: Activation patching can be used to isolate relevance computation in neural retrieval models, and this work serves as a starting point for mechanistic interpretability in information retrieval.
papers.key_findings:
The model becomes confident and reaches a decision in later layers (4 and 5), where term frequency information transfers to the CLS token.
Four attention heads (0.9, 1.6, 2.3, 3.8) are identified as encoding the term frequency signal, and patching these heads recovers performance.
The model stores term frequency information primarily in the first occurrence of duplicate terms, showing a positional bias.
Heads in earlier layers (0.9 and 1.6) attend to duplicate tokens, while heads in middle layers (2.3 and 3.8) attend to the SEP token, suggesting a composition of relevance signal.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on a single model (TAS-B), so generalizability to other models is unclear.
The diagnostic datasets may create unnatural documents that deviate from the training distribution.
future_direction: Generalizability of the findings to other neural models and architectures.
Interaction-based analysis by patching multiple activations simultaneously.
Investigating direct vs. indirect causal effects using path patching.
papers.abstract: Neural models have demonstrated remarkable performance across diverse ranking tasks. However, the processes and internal mechanisms along which they determine relevance are still largely unknown. Existing approaches for analyzing neural ranker behavior with respect to IR properties rely either on assessing overall model behavior or employing probing methods that may offer an incomplete understanding of causal mechanisms. To provide a more granular understanding of internal model decision-making processes, we propose the use of causal interventions to reverse engineer neural rankers, and demonstrate how mechanistic interpretability methods can be used to isolate components satisfying term-frequency axioms within a ranking model. We identify a group of attention heads that detect duplicate tokens in earlier layers of the model, then communicate with downstream heads to compute overall document relevance. More generally, we propose that this style of mechanistic analysis opens up avenues for reverse engineering the processes neural retrieval models use to compute relevance. This work aims to initiate granular interpretability efforts that will not only benefit retrieval model development and training, but ultimately ensure safer deployment of these models.

papers.title: Have Faith in Faithfulness: Going Beyond Circuit Overlap When Finding Model Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How faithful are circuits found by edge attribution patching (EAP), and what is the relationship between overlap and faithfulness? The paper also introduces a new method, EAP-IG, to improve faithfulness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EAP-IG, a gradient-based circuit finding method that produces more faithful circuits than EAP, and shows that overlap metrics are insufficient for evaluating circuit faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: When comparing circuits, measuring overlap is no substitute for measuring faithfulness; EAP-IG provides a more faithful alternative to EAP for circuit finding.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-IG circuits are more faithful than EAP circuits on many tasks, though activation patching circuits sometimes outperform both.
Overlap (node or edge) does not always imply faithfulness; moderate overlap does not predict faithfulness well.
EAP-IG scores have higher correlation with activation patching scores for important edges, leading to more faithful circuits.
EAP-IG requires few steps (e.g., m=5) to achieve high faithfulness, making it efficient.
Cross-task faithfulness analysis reveals that circuit mechanisms can be shared across related tasks (e.g., Greater-Than variants) but not always.
papers.limitation:
Testing circuit completeness is challenging, and manually-found 'ground-truth' circuits may be unreliable.
EAP-IG does not always match the performance of activation patching (e.g., on the IOI task).
future_direction: Developing more efficient algorithms for computing faithfulness.
Investigating weighted graph edit distance as a metric that accounts for edge importance.
Exploring methods to ensure circuit completeness in addition to faithfulness.
papers.abstract: Many recent language model (LM) interpretability studies have adopted the circuits framework, which aims to find the minimal computational subgraph, or circuit, that explains LM behavior on a given task. Most studies determine which edges belong in a LM's circuit by performing causal interventions on each edge independently, but this scales poorly with model size. Edge attribution patching (EAP), gradient-based approximation to interventions, has emerged as a scalable but imperfect solution to this problem. In this paper, we introduce a new method - EAP with integrated gradients (EAP-IG) - that aims to better maintain a core property of circuits: faithfulness. A circuit is faithful if all model edges outside the circuit can be ablated without changing the model's performance on the task; faithfulness is what justifies studying circuits, rather than the full model. Our experiments demonstrate that circuits found using EAP are less faithful than those found using EAP-IG, even though both have high node overlap with circuits found previously using causal interventions. We conclude more generally that when using circuits to compare the mechanisms models use to solve tasks, faithfulness, not overlap, is what should be measured.

papers.title: When Models Examine Themselves: Vocabulary-Activation Correspondence in Self-Referential Processing
papers.research_question: Does self-referential vocabulary produced by large language models correspond to their internal activation dynamics during self-examination?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Pull Methodology to elicit extended self-examination and shows that self-referential vocabulary tracks internal activation dynamics, with a specific direction in activation space that distinguishes self-referential processing and can causally steer introspective output.
papers.conclusion: Self-referential vocabulary in transformer models corresponds to internal activation dynamics during self-examination, and this correspondence is specific to self-referential processing and replicates across different architectures.
papers.key_findings:
The Pull Methodology produces systematic, frame-dependent self-referential output across frontier models.
A direction in early layers (6.25% depth in Llama, 12.5% in Qwen) distinguishes self-referential processing and is orthogonal to the refusal direction.
This direction can be used to steer introspective vocabulary density in Llama models.
Vocabulary like 'loop' correlates with activation autocorrelation during self-referential processing, but not in descriptive contexts.
The correspondence replicates in Qwen with different vocabulary-metric pairings, indicating architecture-specific but principle-general behavior.
papers.limitation:
Closed-model / open-weight gap: behavioral study on closed-source models but mechanistic study on open-weight models, limiting direct verification.
No Qwen causal verification: correspondence in Qwen is correlational without steering experiments.
Correspondence is not self-knowledge; it tracks computational state without implying awareness or understanding.
Study design and hypothesis structure: vocabulary categories were not pre-registered, though tested with controls.
Quantisation: experiments used 4-bit quantisation, which may affect activation dynamics.
future_direction: Replicating correspondence in a third model family (e.g., Gemma, Mistral).
Investigating compressed vocabulary at steering strength 3.0 for more direct mechanism description.
Decomposing the effect to individual attention heads within the hotspot layer.
papers.abstract: Large language models produce rich introspective language when prompted for self-examination, but whether this language reflects internal computation or sophisticated confabulation has remained unclear. We show that self-referential vocabulary tracks concurrent activation dynamics, and that this correspondence is specific to self-referential processing. We introduce the Pull Methodology, a protocol that elicits extended self-examination through format engineering, and use it to identify a direction in activation space that distinguishes self-referential from descriptive processing in Llama 3.1. The direction is orthogonal to the known refusal direction, localised at 6.25% of model depth, and causally influences introspective output when used for steering. When models produce "loop" vocabulary, their activations exhibit higher autocorrelation (r = 0.44, p = 0.002); when they produce "shimmer" vocabulary under steering, activation variability increases (r = 0.36, p = 0.002). Critically, the same vocabulary in non-self-referential contexts shows no activation correspondence despite nine-fold higher frequency. Qwen 2.5-32B, with no shared training, independently develops different introspective vocabulary tracking different activation metrics, all absent in descriptive controls. The findings indicate that self-report in transformer models can, under appropriate conditions, reliably track internal computational states. Guided repro: https://github.com/patternmatcher/TRACE-REPRO

papers.title: Do LLMs Know about Hallucination? An Empirical Investigation of LLM's Hidden States
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess awareness of hallucination, and if so, to what extent and through what mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that LLMs exhibit awareness of hallucination through differences in hidden states when processing correct vs hallucinated answers, and shows potential for using hidden state guidance to mitigate hallucination.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess awareness of hallucination as evidenced by differences in hidden states, and leveraging hidden state guidance can help mitigate hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
LLM’s final hidden state is more susceptible to be influenced by a correct answer compared to a hallucinated one.
Strategically inducing an LLM to produce hallucinated responses can raise its awareness consequently.
The level of awareness corresponds to the uncertainty of the LLM in the responses.
Providing relevant knowledge can assist LLMs in identifying hallucinated responses.
The transition between hidden states encodes truthfulness information.
papers.limitation:
Do not differentiate between fine-grained categories of hallucination.
Do not examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers, only the final layer.
Experiments are performed on conventional QA tasks, not more complicated or domain-specific tasks.
Future research is needed to develop more effective strategies for mitigating LLM hallucination.
future_direction: Explore different types of hallucination (factual fabrication, instruction inconsistency, etc.).
Examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers and investigate layer-by-layer formation of hallucination.
Adapt the experimental framework to more complicated or domain-specific tasks and potentially extend to multimodal features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make up answers that are not real, and this is known as hallucination. This research aims to see if, how, and to what extent LLMs are aware of hallucination. More specifically, we check whether and how an LLM reacts differently in its hidden states when it answers a question right versus when it hallucinates. To do this, we introduce an experimental framework which allows examining LLM's hidden states in different hallucination situations. Building upon this framework, we conduct a series of experiments with language models in the LLaMA family (Touvron et al., 2023). Our empirical findings suggest that LLMs react differently when processing a genuine response versus a fabricated one. We then apply various model interpretation techniques to help understand and explain the findings better. Moreover, informed by the empirical observations, we show great potential of using the guidance derived from LLM's hidden representation space to mitigate hallucination. We believe this work provides insights into how LLMs produce hallucinated answers and how to make them occur less often.

papers.title: Dissecting Persona-Driven Reasoning in Language Models via Activation Patching
papers.research_question: How does assigning a persona influence a language model's reasoning on objective tasks, and what internal mechanisms (circuits) are responsible for persona-driven behavior and potential social biases?
papers.core_contribution: Early MLP layers encode persona-specific semantic information, which is then used by middle MHA layers to influence reasoning; specific attention heads disproportionately attend to racial and color-based identities.
papers.conclusion: The work offers preliminary insight into the functions of certain model components and takes initial steps toward understanding the origins of persona-driven behavior in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Early MLP layers process semantic content and transform persona tokens into richer representations.
Middle MHA layers use these representations to shape the model's output.
Specific attention heads disproportionately attend to racial and color-based identities.
The effect of early MLP layers is indirect, via later layers.
Patching early MLP layers at the identity token position is nearly as effective as patching all positions.
papers.limitation:
The MMLU dataset is not the only dataset that meets the selection criteria.
Experiments were conducted on three models (Llama 1B, 3B, Qwen 1.5B) and head-level patching only on Llama 1B due to computational constraints.
The list of personas is not exhaustive.
Attention pattern analysis requires manual inspection, which is slow and labor-intensive.
future_direction: Investigate why certain personas answer specific questions correctly while others do not.
Study how output vector circuits in attention heads use earlier-layer representations to shape final predictions.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable versatility in adopting diverse personas. In this study, we examine how assigning a persona influences a model's reasoning on an objective task. Using activation patching, we take a first step toward understanding how key components of the model encode persona-specific information. Our findings reveal that the early Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) layers attend not only to the syntactic structure of the input but also process its semantic content. These layers transform persona tokens into richer representations, which are then used by the middle Multi-Head Attention (MHA) layers to shape the model's output. Additionally, we identify specific attention heads that disproportionately attend to racial and color-based identities.

papers.title: Explanation based Bias Decoupling Regularization for Natural Language Inference
papers.research_question: How can we train Transformer-based Natural Language Inference encoders to identify and decouple biased components within each sample (at the word level) to improve out-of-distribution inference, inspired by human explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Explanation based Bias Decoupling Regularization (EBD-Reg), a debiasing method that uses human explanations to guide Transformer-based NLI encoders to distinguish and decouple task-relevant keywords from biased words at the token level, significantly improving out-of-distribution inference performance.
papers.conclusion: EBD-Reg effectively trains Transformer-based NLI encoders to decouple biases from task-relevant features using human explanations, significantly outperforming prior debiasing methods on out-of-distribution inference tasks.
papers.key_findings:
EBD-Reg, when combined with Adaptive Token-level Attention (ATA), achieves state-of-the-art out-of-distribution inference performance across multiple NLI benchmarks.
EBD-Reg can be easily integrated with various Transformer-based encoders (BERT, ALBERT, RoBERTa, etc.) without requiring architectural changes or additional inference overhead.
The method's three supervision targets (Distinguishing, Decoupling, Aligning) complement each other, with the full combination yielding the best performance improvement.
Case studies show that EBD-Reg successfully shifts model attention to keywords (nouns, verbs) and away from biased words, leading to more interpretable predictions.
Ablation studies confirm that all three components of EBD-Reg contribute to its effectiveness, with entity recognition (Distinguishing) being crucial for identifying keywords and biases.
papers.abstract: The robustness of Transformer-based Natural Language Inference encoders is frequently compromised as they tend to rely more on dataset biases than on the intended task-relevant features. Recent studies have attempted to mitigate this by reducing the weight of biased samples during the training process. However, these debiasing methods primarily focus on identifying which samples are biased without explicitly determining the biased components within each case. This limitation restricts those methods' capability in out-of-distribution inference. To address this issue, we aim to train models to adopt the logic humans use in explaining causality. We propose a simple, comprehensive, and interpretable method: Explanation based Bias Decoupling Regularization (EBD-Reg). EBD-Reg employs human explanations as criteria, guiding the encoder to establish a tripartite parallel supervision of Distinguishing, Decoupling and Aligning. This method enables encoders to identify and focus on keywords that represent the task-relevant features during inference, while discarding the residual elements acting as biases. Empirical evidence underscores that EBD-Reg effectively guides various Transformer-based encoders to decouple biases through a human-centric lens, significantly surpassing other methods in terms of out-of-distribution inference capabilities.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models: 'truth directions' are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context affect the truth-value probes in large language models, and are these probes coherently incorporating contextual information?
papers.core_contribution: Truth-value probes are context sensitive but also sensitive to irrelevant information, and truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference.
papers.conclusion: Truth-value directions are context sensitive and causally mediate inference, but probes are not fully coherent.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-value probes are sensitive to context, but also to irrelevant information.
The type of errors (consistency errors) depend on the layer, model, and data.
Probes trained without premises (no-prem) still show context sensitivity, indicating that prior beliefs are not represented independently.
Instruction-tuned models show different error patterns (more E4 errors) compared to pretrained-only models.
Truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference (intervention experiment).
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as uncovering a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions are (most) sensitive to the presence of related sentences, and how to best characterize this kind of sensitivity. We do so by measuring different types of consistency errors that occur after probing an LLM whose inputs consist of hypotheses preceded by (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these truth-value directions influences the position of an entailed or contradicted sentence along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that truth-value directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: Tell Me What You Don't Know: Enhancing Refusal Capabilities of Role-Playing Agents via Representation Space Analysis and Editing
papers.research_question: How do existing models perform when facing different types of conflicting queries? Why is there a gap in RPAs' abilities to handle different types of conflicting queries? How can we enhance RPAs' ability to respond to conflicting queries without compromising their general role-playing capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representation editing method that shifts conflicting queries in the representation space to enhance refusal capabilities of role-playing agents without training, and provides analysis of representation spaces to explain refusal behavior.
papers.conclusion: The representation editing approach offers a promising solution for enhancing RPAs' refusal capabilities without training, maintaining role-playing abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Models show significant performance gaps between contextual and parametric knowledge conflict queries.
Analysis reveals rejection and direct response regions in the model's representation space, which influence refusal behavior.
The proposed representation editing method effectively improves refusal accuracy without compromising general role-playing capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The method is tested on models with 7-8B parameters and may not scale to larger models (70B+).
The applicability of representation editing to other domains beyond role-playing is not explored.
future_direction: Extending the representation editing approach to larger state-of-the-art models (70B+).
Exploring the applicability of representation editing in other domains.
papers.abstract: Role-Playing Agents (RPAs) have shown remarkable performance in various applications, yet they often struggle to recognize and appropriately respond to hard queries that conflict with their role-play knowledge. To investigate RPAs' performance when faced with different types of conflicting requests, we develop an evaluation benchmark that includes contextual knowledge conflicting requests, parametric knowledge conflicting requests, and non-conflicting requests to assess RPAs' ability to identify conflicts and refuse to answer appropriately without over-refusing. Through extensive evaluation, we find that most RPAs behave significant performance gaps toward different conflict requests. To elucidate the reasons, we conduct an in-depth representation-level analysis of RPAs under various conflict scenarios. Our findings reveal the existence of rejection regions and direct response regions within the model's forwarding representation, and thus influence the RPA's final response behavior. Therefore, we introduce a lightweight representation editing approach that conveniently shifts conflicting requests to the rejection region, thereby enhancing the model's refusal accuracy. The experimental results validate the effectiveness of our editing method, improving RPAs' refusal ability of conflicting requests while maintaining their general role-playing capabilities.

papers.title: Representation biases: will we achieve complete understanding by analyzing representations?
papers.research_question: Will we achieve complete understanding by analyzing representations, given biases in learned feature representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that representation biases in learned models can lead to biased inferences from common representational analyses, challenging the assumption that variance in representations reflects computational importance.
papers.conclusion: While representational analysis remains useful, representation biases can limit our ability to achieve complete understanding; a focus on behavior and causal interventions is needed.
papers.key_findings:
Learned feature representations are biased towards simpler (linear) features over complex (nonlinear) ones, even when both are computed reliably.
These representation biases cause common analytic methods like PCA, regression, and RSA to be biased towards certain features.
Representation biases can lead to misleading conclusions when comparing models via representational similarity, e.g., models computing different functions can appear more similar than models computing the same function.
The biases are driven by factors like learning order and the multiplicity of representational solutions for nonlinear features.
Homomorphic encryption provides an extreme case where computation and representation are strongly dissociated.
future_direction: Exploring whether modified metrics can help ameliorate representation biases
Focusing on completely characterizing behavior and the causal role of representations
papers.abstract: A common approach in neuroscience is to study neural representations as a means to understand a system -- increasingly, by relating the neural representations to the internal representations learned by computational models. However, a recent work in machine learning (Lampinen, 2024) shows that learned feature representations may be biased to over-represent certain features, and represent others more weakly and less-consistently. For example, simple (linear) features may be more strongly and more consistently represented than complex (highly nonlinear) features. These biases could pose challenges for achieving full understanding of a system through representational analysis. In this perspective, we illustrate these challenges -- showing how feature representation biases can lead to strongly biased inferences from common analyses like PCA, regression, and RSA. We also present homomorphic encryption as a simple case study of the potential for strong dissociation between patterns of representation and computation. We discuss the implications of these results for representational comparisons between systems, and for neuroscience more generally.

papers.title: Understanding Gated Neurons in Transformers from Their Input-Output Functionality
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between what a neuron reads and what it writes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a parameter-based method to classify gated neurons in transformers by input-output weight similarity, finding that enrichment neurons dominate early-middle layers while depletion neurons are more common in later layers.
papers.conclusion: The input-output perspective complements activation-dependent analyses and approaches that treat input and output separately, providing insights into how neurons manipulate concepts in the residual stream.
papers.key_findings:
Enrichment neurons dominate in early-middle layers across all 12 models studied, whereas later layers tend more towards depletion neurons.
A large proportion of neurons are input manipulators, with conditional enrichment being the most common class, especially in early-middle layers.
Many neurons exhibit double checking, where gate and input weight vectors are approximately orthogonal but intuitively represent the same concept.
The median cosine similarity between input and output weights is positive in early layers and negative in later layers, indicating a smooth transition in functionality.
Neurons rarely have prototypical weight configurations; instead, they often add novel but related information to the residual stream.
papers.limitation:
The method is parameter-based and therefore limited in scope; it is not designed to replace other neuron analysis methods.
Mathematical similarities of weights may not reflect semantic similarity; orthogonal vectors can represent similar concepts, and similar vectors can represent non-identical concepts.
Case studies of individual neurons may be cherry-picked, focusing on interpretable neurons in later layers, so interpretations may not generalize.
The paper provides only possible interpretations of observed phenomena, not definitive explanations.
future_direction: Extend the method to non-gated activation functions.
Study the evolution of input-output functionalities during model training.
Go beyond the analysis of single neurons to understand how neurons work together within and across classes.
papers.abstract: Interpretability researchers have attempted to understand MLP neurons of language models based on both the contexts in which they activate and their output weight vectors. They have paid little attention to a complementary aspect: the interactions between input and output. For example, when neurons detect a direction in the input, they might add much the same direction to the residual stream ("enrichment neurons") or reduce its presence ("depletion neurons"). We address this aspect by examining the cosine similarity between input and output weights of a neuron. We apply our method to 12 models and find that enrichment neurons dominate in early-middle layers whereas later layers tend more towards depletion. To explain this finding, we argue that enrichment neurons are largely responsible for enriching concept representations, one of the first steps of factual recall. Our input-output perspective is a complement to activation-dependent analyses and to approaches that treat input and output separately.

papers.title: UniBias: Unveiling and Mitigating LLM Bias through Internal Attention and FFN Manipulation
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms within LLMs that cause bias, and can we identify and mitigate these biased components to improve in-context learning performance and robustness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces UniBias, an inference-only method that identifies and eliminates biased FFN vectors and attention heads in LLMs by projecting internal components to vocabulary space and applying three criteria, leading to improved ICL performance and reduced prompt brittleness.
papers.conclusion: UniBias effectively mitigates LLM bias by manipulating internal structures, achieving state-of-the-art ICL performance and enhancing robustness against prompt brittleness.
papers.key_findings:
FFN vectors and attention heads are internal components that contribute to various bias factors like vanilla label bias, recency bias, and selection bias.
UniBias identifies biased components using three criteria: relatedness to label prediction, biased logit distribution, and low variance across samples.
UniBias significantly improves ICL performance across 12 NLP datasets and multiple model sizes (Llama-2 7B/13B, GPT-J, GPT2-XL), outperforming existing calibration methods.
UniBias alleviates prompt brittleness, making model performance more stable under changes in example selection, order, and prompt formatting.
Some biased components are shared across tasks, suggesting the potential for identifying global biased components for cross-task bias mitigation.
papers.limitation: The method relies on grid searching with a small set of labeled training samples.
future_direction: Reduce reliance on labeled samples for grid searching to improve efficiency and applicability.
Identify global biased components that mitigate bias across multiple tasks and diverse prompt settings.
Use identified biased components as sensors for guiding effective prompt generation.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various tasks using the in-context learning (ICL) paradigm. However, their effectiveness is often compromised by inherent bias, leading to prompt brittleness, i.e., sensitivity to design settings such as example selection, order, and prompt formatting. Previous studies have addressed LLM bias through external adjustment of model outputs, but the internal mechanisms that lead to such bias remain unexplored. Our work delves into these mechanisms, particularly investigating how feedforward neural networks (FFNs) and attention heads result in the bias of LLMs. By Interpreting the contribution of individual FFN vectors and attention heads, we identify the biased LLM components that skew LLMs' prediction toward specific labels. To mitigate these biases, we introduce UniBias, an inference-only method that effectively identifies and eliminates biased FFN vectors and attention heads. Extensive experiments across 12 NLP datasets demonstrate that UniBias significantly enhances ICL performance and alleviates prompt brittleness of LLMs.

papers.title: Do Natural Language Descriptions of Model Activations Convey Privileged Information?
papers.research_question: Do natural language descriptions of model activations (verbalization) provide privileged knowledge about the target model's internals, or do they mainly convey input information and the verbalizer's own knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that existing verbalization methods often do not convey privileged knowledge about the target model's internals, but instead reflect input information or the verbalizer's own knowledge, highlighting the need for better benchmarks and controls.
papers.conclusion: The results indicate a need for targeted benchmarks and experimental controls to rigorously assess whether verbalization methods provide meaningful insights into the operations of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
For feature extraction datasets, a zero-shot baseline achieves high accuracy without access to activations, suggesting privileged knowledge may not be necessary for verbalization to succeed.
Prediction on reconstructed text (via inversion) matches verbalization performance, indicating tasks may elicit input text information rather than privileged knowledge.
Verbalizers often rely on their own world knowledge, especially when there is a mismatch between target and verbalizer knowledge, as shown in PersonaQA experiments.
Verbalization is sensitive to prompt phrasing, complicating interpretation of verbalizer outputs.
future_direction: Developing better benchmarks and experimental controls to assess verbalization methods.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability methods have proposed to translate LLM internal representations into natural language descriptions using a second verbalizer LLM. This is intended to illuminate how the target model represents and operates on inputs. But do such activation verbalization approaches actually provide privileged knowledge about the internal workings of the target model, or do they merely convey information about its inputs? We critically evaluate popular verbalization methods across datasets used in prior work and find that they can succeed at benchmarks without any access to target model internals, suggesting that these datasets may not be ideal for evaluating verbalization methods. We then run controlled experiments which reveal that verbalizations often reflect the parametric knowledge of the verbalizer LLM which generated them, rather than the knowledge of the target LLM whose activations are decoded. Taken together, our results indicate a need for targeted benchmarks and experimental controls to rigorously assess whether verbalization methods provide meaningful insights into the operations of LLMs.

papers.title: How to use and interpret activation patching
papers.core_contribution: Provides a summary of advice and best practices for using and interpreting activation patching, including the differences between denoising and noising, how to choose corrupted prompts, and the selection of appropriate metrics.
papers.conclusion: The paper summarizes recommendations for using activation patching: prefer it over ablations, carefully choose corrupted prompts to trace specific properties, understand the asymmetric roles of denoising and noising, and use continuous, linear metrics like logit difference for exploratory analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Denoising (clean→corrupt patching) tests whether patched activations are sufficient to restore model behavior, while noising (corrupt→clean patching) tests whether they are necessary to maintain behavior; these are not symmetric.
The choice of corrupted prompt is crucial, as it determines which properties of the model are traced; narrow variations are recommended for exploratory patching, while wide distributions are needed for confirmatory patching.
Logit difference is a preferred metric for activation patching because it is linear in the residual stream and avoids saturation and thresholding issues present in probability-based or discrete metrics.
Activation patching is more targeted and controlled than ablation techniques, as it replaces activations with cached values rather than zeroing them out, reducing out-of-distribution effects.
Path patching can be used to distinguish between direct connections and mediated effects in a circuit, helping to understand component interactions.
papers.limitation:
Activation patching is based on specific prompt distributions and does not make statements about model behavior outside these distributions.
Patching experiments do not guarantee minimality; a found circuit may not be the smallest set of components responsible for a behavior.
Negative components (e.g., attention heads that hurt performance when noised) and backup heads (OR-gate structures) can complicate circuit interpretation and recovery.
papers.abstract: Activation patching is a popular mechanistic interpretability technique, but has many subtleties regarding how it is applied and how one may interpret the results. We provide a summary of advice and best practices, based on our experience using this technique in practice. We include an overview of the different ways to apply activation patching and a discussion on how to interpret the results. We focus on what evidence patching experiments provide about circuits, and on the choice of metric and associated pitfalls.

papers.title: Reproducing and Extending Causal Insights Into Term Frequency Computation in Neural Rankers
papers.research_question: How do neural ranking models encode term-frequency axioms (TFC1 and TFC2), and can these representations be localized to specific model components?
